Simple cause and effect connectives and three or four concrete examples

sections.heading: Paper 1: two short tasks reward control, not ambition
paragraphs: Arabic ab initio Paper 1 runs for an hour and asks for two written tasks rather than one extended piece, each chosen from options and each in a named text type. Each task is short, in the region of 70 to 150 words. That shape matters more than it appears, because it changes what good practice looks like. A beginner practising one long piece a fortnight is training the wrong thing. Two short, controlled, complete pieces every week is the right habit.

Length discipline is the first lesson. A beginner who writes past the expected length does not earn more marks and does lose control: the accuracy drops, the tenses drift, and the text type convention gets forgotten halfway through. We practise writing to the length and then stopping, which students find unnatural and which protects the language marks. Finishing both tasks inside the hour is itself a skill, since the second task is where candidates run out of time.

Text type still counts at this level. A short message, a postcard, an email, a notice and a blog entry open and close differently, and the marks attached to audience, purpose and register are available to a student with very limited Arabic. A page of conventions per text type is about the most efficient revision material an ab initio candidate has, and it is the sort of thing a tutor can get into place in two or three sessions. The conventions do not change between years, so once a student has them written down they stop being revision and become a checklist.

sections.heading: Paper 2 is half the grade and the hardest half to self-study
paragraphs: Listening and reading together carry 50% of the ab initio grade. At beginner level both fail for reasons that have nothing to do with how much vocabulary the student has learned. Listening fails on segmentation: a student who knows a word on the page cannot find it inside connected speech, because they cannot hear where one word ends and the next begins. Reading fails on panic: an unfamiliar word stops the eye, and the student rereads the same line instead of moving on and inferring.

Both have specific drills. For listening, take ten-second spans rather than whole passages, transcribe what was heard including the gaps, replay, fill in what can be filled, then read the transcript. Twenty minutes three times a week is better than a long session at the weekend, and progress is audible to the student within a fortnight, which matters for a beginner's morale. Numbers, days and times are drilled separately, because they carry a disproportionate share of the answers.

For reading, the habit to install is scanning for what is known and inferring around what is not. A beginner's instinct is to read every word in order and stall at the first unknown one. The counter-habit is to find the three words you recognise, locate the question's target between them, and answer. It is a technique rather than a language skill, which is why it improves faster than anything else on the paper and why it belongs in the first month rather than the last.

sections.heading: The oral: a photograph, a conversation, and one real skill
paragraphs: The ab initio individual oral is internally assessed and worth a quarter of the grade. The student describes a photograph connected to one of the five themes, answers follow-up questions on it, then talks about at least one further theme. Marks cover language, message and interactive skills. A beginner can score respectably here with a small amount of Arabic, provided they have practised on photographs they have never seen before rather than rehearsing one they have.

The skill that actually separates candidates is handling incomprehension. A beginner will not understand some questions. A student who freezes loses the interactive marks and the conversation never recovers. A student who has drilled three phrases for asking something to be repeated, slowed down or rephrased keeps the exchange alive and keeps scoring. Those phrases are perhaps fifteen words of Arabic in total, and they are worth more marks than any fifteen words of topic vocabulary.

The rest is deliberately unglamorous. Describe what is in the photograph, say where it is, say what the people are doing, then say something simple about the theme behind it. Four moves, learned as a sequence, applied to any image. We record every rehearsal and play it back before saying anything, because students hear their own hesitations more honestly than they accept being told about them, and the pauses shorten once they have heard them. Three recordings across three weeks is usually enough for a beginner to stop filling silence in English, which is itself worth marks under the language criterion.
bullets: Practise on unseen photographs, never on a rehearsed one
Drill clarification phrases until they are automatic
Use a fixed four-move description sequence for any image
Play the recording back before any tutor comment

sections.heading: What ab initio does for the Diploma, and what it does not
paragraphs: Ab initio satisfies the Group 2 requirement and contributes its points to the Diploma total like any Standard Level subject. What it cannot do is be a Higher Level, because no HL exists, so the three HL subjects must come from elsewhere. Families planning a subject grid late sometimes discover this after choices have been submitted, and it is worth checking against the grid in DP1 rather than assuming the Group 2 slot is flexible.

For university purposes, ab initio is a beginner's language qualification and should be described as one. It is not evidence of working proficiency in Arabic, and no page should suggest otherwise. Where a UAE university or a Ministry of Education equivalency process is in view, the requirements are set by the institution and the authority, not by us: the British-track equivalency rules published for GCSE, IGCSE and A Level are specific and documented, while no IB points figure for equivalency should be quoted without reading it on the Ministry's own site. Check with the admissions office and the attestation authority directly.

What ab initio does deliver, for a student living in Dubai, is unusually practical. A beginner in a Spanish class in Manchester cannot use the language on the way home. A beginner in Arabic in Dubai can read a shop sign, follow a greeting, and use a handful of phrases in the week they learn them. That turns a required subject into one with visible returns, and in our experience it is the difference between a student who coasts to a 4 and one who works for a 6.

sections.heading: Cost, delivery and what the first month looks like
paragraphs: Published platform and agency rate cards, together with Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, put the Dubai market at roughly AED 45-150 an hour for budget or university-student tutors, AED 150-300 for a qualified online subject tutor, AED 200-450 and above for an IB or IGCSE specialist, and AED 180-500 for an in-home visit where travel sits inside the billed hour. Monthly online packages around AED 799 for eight sessions appear in the same market. Those are October 2026 market figures, not IB Gram prices.

For ab initio specifically, the shape of the spend differs from other subjects. The script phase wants two short sessions a week for about two months, which is more frequent and shorter than a standard weekly booking, then settles to one session a week for topic coverage. Families who plan the first two months properly tend to need fewer hours in DP2, because a student who reads fluently by the spring of DP1 can use ordinary classroom teaching, and a student who cannot never catches up to it.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Ab initio lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. We start with a free trial lesson, with no card required, and that trial is spent checking two things: whether your child is genuinely a beginner, and whether they can recognise ten letters by the end of the hour. Both answers are useful before anybody commits to a term.

process.title: Answer the eligibility question first
process.description: How many years was Arabic on your child's timetable, in which school system, and what did those lessons contain? The MYP phase or the previous school's language record settles it faster than any assessment. A student with substantial prior Arabic belongs in Arabic B and we will say so.

process.title: Free trial spent on the alphabet
process.description: The trial session teaches a first group of letters and finds out how quickly recognition sticks. That tells us whether the script phase is six weeks or twelve, which is the only number that matters for planning. The trial requires no card and the plan is yours regardless.

process.title: Two short sessions a week for the script phase
process.description: Forty-five minutes twice weekly for roughly two months, live online in Gulf Standard Time. Letter groups, handwriting, reading aloud, and vowels withdrawn in stages. This is the phase where frequency matters more than total hours, so we would rather have two short slots than one long one.

process.title: Switch to weekly topic coverage with a written list
process.description: Once reading holds, one session a week works through the twenty prescribed topics in a written order, each block closing with a short Paper 1 style task. The coverage list is shared, so in DP2 a family can see which topics are done rather than hoping they all are.

process.title: Oral and listening block before the school window
process.description: Five or six sessions in the weeks before the school records the oral, working on unseen photographs and on clarification phrases. Listening drills continue in parallel at twenty minutes three times a week, which the student does alone between sessions.

whyPoints.title: A straight answer on eligibility
whyPoints.description: Ab initio is for genuine beginners and the school decides. Where a child has had years of timetabled Dubai school Arabic, we say that Arabic B is the course and remedial work is the plan, even though it is not the answer the family came for.

whyPoints.title: The script treated as real content
whyPoints.description: Two months on letter forms, handwriting and withdrawing short vowels in stages, not a fortnight of alphabet worksheets before the course starts. A student who still decodes word by word in DP2 lost those marks in the first term of DP1.

whyPoints.title: Topic coverage you can audit
whyPoints.description: Twenty prescribed topics, a written list, and sessions marked off against it. Vocabulary at beginner level is topic-bound, so an uncovered topic is a cliff on one specific task rather than a general weakness. Gaps should be visible, not discovered in an exam.

whyPoints.title: Frequency matched to the phase
whyPoints.description: Two short sessions a week while reading is forming, one weekly session once it holds. Recognition builds through spaced repetition, so a single long weekly slot in the early phase produces a student who can read on Tuesday and not on Friday.

whyPoints.title: Clarification drilled before vocabulary
whyPoints.description: Fifteen words of Arabic for asking a question to be repeated or rephrased are worth more marks in the oral than any fifteen words of topic vocabulary, because they keep the conversation and the interactive marks alive when comprehension fails.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and claims stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one and online over live video in Gulf Standard Time. No tutor is sent to a UAE address, no UAE office exists, and IB Gram claims no licence or accreditation from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE or the IB.

faqs.question: Can my child switch to Arabic ab initio to get an easier grade?
faqs.answer: Generally no, and it is worth understanding why before asking the school. Ab initio is designed for students with little or no previous experience of the language, and the school decides eligibility. A child who has had Arabic as an additional language on a Dubai school timetable for several years has prior experience on record, however little they retained. The course is a starting point rather than a difficulty setting. For that student the realistic plan is remedial work inside Arabic B, which can move a grade substantially and does not put the Diploma coordinator in an impossible position.

faqs.question: Is there a Higher Level option for Arabic ab initio?
faqs.answer: No. Arabic ab initio exists at Standard Level only, across roughly 150 recommended teaching hours. That has a practical consequence for subject planning that families sometimes miss: the Diploma requires three subjects at Higher Level, and none of them can be this one, so all three have to come from the other groups. If the subject grid was built on the assumption that Group 2 could supply an HL, it needs revisiting with the Diploma coordinator, and DP1 is the time to do that rather than DP2.

faqs.question: How long does it take to read Arabic from scratch?
faqs.answer: For a motivated sixteen-year-old working with a tutor twice a week, slow reading of simple unvowelled text is a realistic target inside eight to ten weeks. Recognition of all the letter forms comes sooner, usually four to six weeks. Fluent reading takes considerably longer and is not the DP1 goal. What matters is that the student can start a sentence rather than stall at it, because every later part of the course, including listening practice and Paper 1 tasks, assumes reading works. Frequency drives this more than total hours.

faqs.question: Why are short vowels taught and then taken away?
faqs.answer: Because teaching materials print them and real Arabic mostly does not. A beginner trained exclusively on fully vowelled text reads confidently until the first authentic passage, where the support vanishes and so does their reading. So we withdraw the vowels in stages: fully marked, then marked only on unfamiliar words, then absent. The student notices the change and finds it uncomfortable for a fortnight. The alternative is discovering in DP2 that none of their reading practice transferred to anything the exam will actually put in front of them.

faqs.question: What does Arabic ab initio Paper 1 ask for?
faqs.answer: Two short written tasks rather than one extended piece, within an hour, each chosen from options and each in a named text type such as a message, a postcard, an email, a notice or a blog entry. Each task is short, in the region of 70 to 150 words. The practical implication is that practice should be two short complete pieces a week, not one long one a fortnight. Writing beyond the expected length earns nothing and costs accuracy, so writing to length and stopping is a skill we drill deliberately.

faqs.question: How many topics are on the Arabic ab initio course?
faqs.answer: Twenty prescribed topics, four inside each of the five themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. Because the syllabus is finite and countable, a family can reasonably ask to see a coverage list and check it against the calendar. That matters at beginner level because vocabulary is topic-bound: a student who has covered fourteen topics is not generally weaker, they are fine on fourteen tasks and stranded on six. We keep the list in writing and mark it off.

faqs.question: How is the ab initio individual oral assessed?
faqs.answer: It is internally assessed by the school, recorded, and worth a quarter of the grade. The student describes a photograph linked to one of the five themes, answers follow-up questions about it, then discusses at least one further theme. Marks cover language, message and interactive skills. A beginner can do well here with modest Arabic if they have practised on photographs they have never seen. The decisive skill is handling a question they do not understand without the conversation collapsing, which is a drill rather than a talent.

faqs.question: What should a beginner do about Arabic listening practice?
faqs.answer: Change the method rather than the material. Take ten-second spans of any clean Modern Standard Arabic recording. Play it, transcribe what was heard including the gaps, replay, fill in what can be filled, replay once more, then read the transcript. At beginner level the bottleneck is segmentation, not vocabulary: the student knows the word on the page and cannot find it inside connected speech. Twenty minutes three times a week beats a long weekend session, and numbers, days and times should be drilled separately because they carry many of the answers.

faqs.question: Does Arabic ab initio count as speaking Arabic for university applications?
faqs.answer: It should be described as a beginner's language qualification, because that is what it is. It satisfies the Diploma's Group 2 requirement and contributes points like any Standard Level subject, but it is not evidence of working proficiency and no honest page would present it as such. Where a UAE university or a Ministry of Education equivalency process is involved, the requirements belong to the institution and the authority. Check them directly with the admissions office and the attestation authority rather than relying on any tutoring provider's summary, including ours.

faqs.question: Is living in Dubai an advantage for a beginner in Arabic?
faqs.answer: A real one, and underused. A beginner studying a language in a country where nobody speaks it practises in a vacuum. In Dubai a student can use a greeting, read a shop sign, order something or follow a short exchange in the same week they learn the words. That turns a required subject into one with visible returns, which is most of what sustains a beginner's effort over eighteen months. We keep spoken local Arabic clearly labelled as separate from the Modern Standard Arabic the exam uses, so the two do not blur.

faqs.question: Will a tutor come to our home in Dubai for ab initio lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Ab initio lessons are taught one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, which for most Dubai families means a weekday evening or a weekend morning. For a beginners' course the format carries a specific advantage: letter forms, handwriting models and short reading texts can be put on a shared screen and revisited, and the oral rehearsal recording is kept for the student to listen back to.

faqs.question: How often should a complete beginner have Arabic lessons?
faqs.answer: Twice a week for forty-five minutes while the writing system is forming, which is roughly the first two months, then once a week for topic coverage. Reading a new script is a recognition skill and recognition builds through repetition spaced across days rather than concentrated in one long sitting. A single ninety-minute weekly session in the early phase produces a student who can read on Tuesday and cannot on Friday. Once reading holds, weekly sessions tied to the prescribed topics are enough, with listening drills done alone between them.

faqs.question: Is ab initio tutoring cheaper than Arabic B tutoring in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Not by the hour. Dubai market rates from published rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table run roughly AED 150-300 for a qualified online subject tutor and AED 200-450 and above for an IB specialist, whatever the course. What differs is the shape of the spend: ab initio wants two short sessions a week for two months and then settles to one, while Arabic B is usually a steady weekly booking. Families who invest properly in the script phase tend to need fewer hours later, because the student can then use ordinary classroom teaching.

faqs.question: My child joined their Dubai school in October. Is it too late to start ab initio?
faqs.answer: No, but the first two months change shape. A mid-year arrival compresses the script phase, so the two weekly short sessions matter more and the reading-aloud habit has to start immediately. The topic coverage list is then built backwards from the school's own schedule rather than forwards from the start of the course, with the high-frequency domestic topics taken first because they recycle into everything later. What is genuinely difficult is arriving in DP2 with no Arabic, which is a conversation to have with the Diploma coordinator about the subject grid.

faqs.question: What will we see in the first month of ab initio sessions?
faqs.answer: Concrete things rather than a grade. By the end of the first month a student should recognise most letter forms in isolation and in words, write their own name and a few sentences legibly, read a short fully vowelled sentence aloud, and use numbers and days without hesitating. Those are checkable at home in five minutes. What should not be expected in a first month is comprehension of recordings or anything resembling conversation, and a tutor claiming otherwise is describing a different student from the one in the room.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-home-tutor.closingHeading: Settle the eligibility question, then start with the alphabet
dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-home-tutor.closingBody: Two questions decide whether ab initio support is the right purchase. Is your child genuinely a beginner, which depends on how many years Arabic sat on their timetable rather than on how much they remember? And how quickly do letter forms stick, which decides whether the script phase runs six weeks or twelve? A free trial lesson answers both, with no card required, and you keep the answer either way. Sessions run one-to-one online in Gulf Standard Time. If the honest answer is that Arabic B is your child's course, we will say so in the first hour.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-online-tuto.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Arabic from a standing start to Diploma Standard Level. They work in Modern Standard Arabic, teach handwriting and letter joining explicitly, and plan against the twenty prescribed topics rather than against a general beginners' textbook.

intro.heading: A beginners' course with a real exam at the end of it
paragraphs: Arabic ab initio is the Diploma's entry point into Arabic for students with little or no previous exposure to the language. It runs at Standard Level only, over the two Diploma years, and it ends in an external examination. Families in Dubai often choose it on the assumption that a beginners' course will be the light option in a heavy Diploma. It is lighter than Arabic B, which is a different and more demanding course, but it is not light. A student starting from zero has to learn a new script, acquire enough vocabulary to handle twenty prescribed topics, and sit a listening paper in a language they did not speak two years earlier.

The course is built around the same five themes as the rest of Group 2, but it narrows them into twenty prescribed topics, four per theme. That narrowing is the single most useful fact about the subject, because it makes the whole syllabus knowable. Unlike Arabic B, where any topic within a theme may appear, ab initio tells you what the examination can ask about. A student who has prepared vocabulary and a few reliable structures for each of the twenty topics has covered the course. Very few beginners are taught it that way, which is why so many arrive at Year 13 with broad, shallow Arabic.

Assessment is split three ways. Paper 1 is writing and carries a quarter: two short tasks, each in the region of 70 to 150 words, from a choice of three, with a text type specified for each. Paper 2 is receptive skills and carries half, with a listening section followed by a reading section in one sitting. The individual oral is internally assessed, carries the final quarter, and starts from a visual stimulus drawn from the prescribed topics before widening into general conversation. Nothing in that model rewards breadth for its own sake, and everything in it rewards accuracy in a limited range.

There is an eligibility question families should settle before anything else. Ab initio is restricted to genuine beginners. A student who has carried Dubai's mandatory school Arabic since primary is, in most schools' judgement, not a beginner, however poor their marks are and however little they feel they know. That restriction catches out a lot of Dubai families, because KHDA requires Arabic in every private school in the emirate whatever the licensed curriculum, so a long record of Arabic lessons exists even where very little Arabic was learned. Ask the Diploma coordinator for the school's position in writing before planning around the course.

Where a student is genuinely eligible, Dubai is a good place to be learning. Arabic is on signage, in lifts, in announcements and in the street, so incidental exposure is constant in a way it would not be in London or Singapore. The limitation is that almost all of that exposure is dialect, while the course assesses Modern Standard Arabic. A tutor who knows the difference can harvest the environment for motivation and listening confidence while keeping the written work firmly on the standard variety the examiner will read.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-online-tuto.programmesIntro: Beginner Arabic looks different in each IB programme, and a Dubai student arriving in the Diploma as a beginner has usually passed through at least one of the others. The notes below cover where the subject sits and what a student typically brings into Year 12 from each.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic ab initio occupies a Group 2 slot at Standard Level and is examined at the end of Year 13. Paper 1 is two short written tasks worth 25 per cent, Paper 2 is listening and reading worth 50 per cent, and the internally assessed individual oral carries 25 per cent. There is no Higher Level route and no literary works requirement, so the whole course is defined by the twenty prescribed topics.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the Diploma is a minority post-16 route, with IB schools accounting for 7 per cent of private-school enrolment against 37 per cent for the UK curriculum on KHDA's 2024-25 figures. A Dubai Diploma cohort is therefore small, and an ab initio class inside it is often four or five students, which affects how much individual attention the school can give to handwriting.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Language acquisition in the MYP runs in phases rather than year groups, and a student can finish the programme in an early phase without that counting as beginner status. Four criteria cover listening, reading, speaking and writing. For a student heading towards ab initio the question is not the phase number but whether any reading and writing of the script was ever assessed.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai MYP cohorts turn over heavily, and students frequently arrive from a school in another emirate or another country with an Arabic record that does not map onto phases. Schools reconstruct a placement in the first weeks of term, which is why two students with identical experience can land in different streams in different Dubai schools.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme includes language development as a core component rather than an examined Group 2 subject. Students build and record their language learning in a portfolio, which suits a beginner who wants functional Arabic for work in the Gulf without an external examination. The standard reached is usually lower than ab initio demands, but the purpose is different.
programmes.countryNote: Only a small number of Dubai schools are authorised for the Career-related Programme, so most families comparing it with the Diploma are also comparing schools. For a student whose plan is to stay and work in the UAE, functional spoken Arabic recorded in a portfolio can be worth more than an examined Standard Level grade.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-online-tuto.subjectsIntro: Beginner Arabic rarely arrives alone in a tuition request. The subjects below are the ones Dubai ab initio students most often need support in at the same time, with a note on what each one competes for in the week.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: The subject of this page. The limiting factor for almost every student is script fluency: a learner who still forms letters slowly cannot finish two written tasks in an hour, however good their vocabulary has become. Handwriting is therefore taught as a timed skill, not as a presentation skill.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The next course up, for students with several years of prior Arabic. Its Paper 1 is one long task rather than two short ones, its topics are not prescribed, and Higher Level requires two literary works in Arabic. Students sometimes move up after a strong first year, which is a conversation to have with the coordinator early.

subjects.name: Spanish ab initio
subjects.description: The commonest alternative beginner language in Dubai IB schools, and worth comparing honestly. The script is already familiar, so the first six months are faster. Arabic repays the extra effort in a Gulf context, which is the trade a family is actually making.

subjects.name: French ab initio
subjects.description: Often available alongside Arabic in the same school. Dubai students usually find the sound-to-spelling relationship the obstacle here, where in Arabic it is the script. The assessment model is identical, so a tutor's planning approach transfers between the two.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Group 1 subject for most Dubai Diploma students. Its text-type work on audience and purpose is directly reusable in ab initio Paper 1, where each short task names a text type. Teaching the concept once in English saves teaching it twice.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Frequently taken alongside a beginner language by students building a broad rather than specialised Diploma. The scheduling point is that its exploration deadline often lands in the same weeks as the ab initio oral window, so one of the two has to be brought forward.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Popular in Dubai and a natural pairing for a student learning Arabic for regional reasons. The workplace topic in the ab initio prescribed list overlaps usefully, and business vocabulary learned in one subject reinforces the other.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Maps onto the sharing the planet theme, where climate, physical geography and environmental issues are prescribed ab initio topics. A student taking both can build Arabic vocabulary on content they already understand, which is far faster than learning concept and language together.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Relevant here because the ab initio individual oral starts from a visual stimulus. Students used to describing and interpreting images handle the presentation far better, and the skill transfers in the other direction too.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: A beginner language is a surprisingly good source of Theory of Knowledge material, since learning a script raises real questions about language and knowledge. The practical overlap is small, but the essay often benefits from an example the student actually lived through.

sections.heading: Who Arabic ab initio is for, and who a school will refuse
paragraphs: Ab initio exists for students with little or no previous experience of the language, and schools enforce that restriction because the course was designed for a particular starting point. A student with years of prior Arabic sitting in an ab initio class distorts the teaching and gains an advantage the course was not built to offer. The practical effect in Dubai is that a long list of Arabic lessons on a school record will usually disqualify a student, and that list exists for nearly every child educated in the emirate, because KHDA requires Arabic in all private schools regardless of the curriculum licensed.

This produces a conversation that goes badly in a lot of Dubai households. The child has had Arabic since Year 1, dislikes it, cannot write a sentence, and wants the beginners' course. The parent sees a reasonable request. The coordinator sees an eligibility rule and says no. Both are right in their own terms, and the argument is not winnable by persistence. What is worth doing is asking the school three precise questions: what evidence of prior study it uses, whether a student transferring from outside the UAE is treated differently, and what the deadline for a Group 2 change is.

Where eligibility is genuine, the usual profile is a student who arrived in Dubai for Year 11 or Year 12 from a system with no Arabic at all. That student has a real advantage over a beginner learning Arabic in Europe, because the language surrounds them, and a real disadvantage in time, because two years is tight for a new script. The planning answer is to compress the foundations: the script taught in the first term rather than across the first year, so that the remaining time can go on the twenty topics that make up the examinable course.

sections.heading: Learning the Arabic script inside a Diploma timetable
paragraphs: The writing system is the first real obstacle and the one most beginner courses under-teach. Arabic has twenty-eight letters, written right to left, with each letter taking different shapes depending on whether it stands alone or sits at the start, middle or end of a word. Six letters do not join to the letter that follows them, which breaks words into segments and confuses learners who expect continuous joining. Short vowels are marked with diacritics in teaching materials and then largely absent from the authentic text the papers use, so a student taught only vowelled text meets an unfamiliar language in the examination.

Speed is the measure that matters, not neatness. Paper 1 asks for two tasks inside one hour, and a learner who forms letters carefully one at a time will not finish. The fix is timed copying and dictation from early on, building to the point where handwriting runs below conscious attention. That is a mechanical, slightly tedious skill, and it is the single clearest predictor of whether a beginner finishes the paper. Reading speed matters just as much in the reading section, where unvowelled text has to be processed under time.

The table below sets out a workable sequence for a student starting in September of Year 12. It is deliberately front-loaded: the script and the first sound-system work compressed into the first term so the remaining five terms can be spent on topics, tasks and the oral. Schools vary in how fast they move, and a tutor's job is to stay ahead of the class rather than behind it, because a beginner who falls behind on the script never catches up on the vocabulary either.

sections.heading: The twenty prescribed topics, which make the syllabus knowable
paragraphs: Ab initio narrows the five Group 2 themes into twenty prescribed topics, four under each theme. That is the structural difference from Arabic B, where any topic within a theme can appear, and it is a significant advantage for a beginner. The examinable content is a finite list. A student who has built a vocabulary core and a few dependable structures for each of the twenty has, in a real sense, finished the course. The work after that is accuracy and speed rather than coverage.

Most beginners are not taught this way. They are taught from a general textbook that introduces useful vocabulary in a sensible order, which is not the same thing as covering twenty named topics to examination depth. The practical difference shows up in Paper 1, where a task on an unprepared topic produces a thin answer from a student with good general Arabic. It shows up again in the oral, where the visual stimulus is drawn from the prescribed topics and a student who has rehearsed images across all twenty is never genuinely surprised.

The table sets out the topics by theme. It is worth printing and keeping, because it doubles as a revision tracker: mark each topic as secure, shaky or untouched after every assessment and the revision plan writes itself. Dubai students often find the social organisation and sharing the planet topics easiest to attach language to, because the local context supplies obvious material, while personal attributes and relationships feel harder despite being simpler, since the vocabulary is abstract.

sections.heading: How the three ab initio components are actually assessed
paragraphs: Paper 1 is productive writing and carries a quarter of the grade. It asks for two tasks rather than one, each in the region of 70 to 150 words, chosen from three options, with a text type specified for each. Short does not mean easy: a 100-word task leaves no room to recover from a misread instruction, and the text type is marked, so a message written as a diary entry loses marks that the Arabic itself did not deserve to lose. Practising at the real length is important, because students who draft long answers in lessons write over-length and unfinished answers in the examination.

Paper 2 carries half the grade and runs as a listening section followed by a reading section in a single sitting. Recordings are played twice and cannot be controlled by the candidate. For a beginner this is the hardest component by a distance, because comprehension of spoken Arabic at natural pace develops slowly and cannot be forced in a final term. Reading is more tractable: the texts are authentic but short, and most lost marks come from unfamiliar vocabulary rather than from complex structures, which makes topic-based vocabulary work directly profitable.

The individual oral is internally assessed by the school, externally moderated, and carries the final quarter. The student prepares from a visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed topics, presents on it, answers follow-up questions, and then moves into a wider conversation. Criteria cover language, the message in response to the stimulus, the message in the conversation, and interactive skills. A beginner's instinct is to give short, safe answers; the interactive criterion punishes exactly that. Teaching a student to extend an answer by one sentence, every time, is worth more marks than another fifty words of vocabulary.

sections.heading: What beginners lose marks on that nobody warns them about
paragraphs: The first is running out of time. Two tasks in an hour is enough for a fluent writer and tight for someone whose handwriting is still deliberate. Students lose whole marks not because they did not know the Arabic but because the second task is three lines long. Timed writing from early in the course is the only fix, and it has to be genuinely timed, with the pen down at the end, because a student who always finishes eventually learns nothing about pace.

The second is ignoring the text type. Each Paper 1 task names what to produce: a message, an email, a notice, a blog post, a set of instructions. Those have conventions, and the conventions are marked. A beginner who writes well-formed general prose for every task has placed a ceiling on their own score. Teaching five or six text types with a model and a checklist for each takes a term and it is the highest-return work available on this course, because the Arabic required is no harder and the marks are simply there.

The third is vocabulary without structure. Beginners collect nouns, which feel like progress, and arrive unable to make a sentence do anything. Four or five reliable structures per topic are worth more than fifty extra nouns: a way to express an opinion, to compare two things, to say what happened yesterday, to say what will happen, and to give a reason. Students who have those can talk about any of the twenty prescribed topics adequately. Students with large vocabularies and no frames stall mid-sentence in the oral, which costs interactive marks.

sections.heading: Is beginner Arabic the right Group 2 choice in a Dubai Diploma?
paragraphs: This is the question most families should ask before booking any tuition at all, and it has an honest answer that depends on the student. Arabic ab initio is harder than beginner Spanish or French for a student whose first language uses the Latin alphabet, because the script is genuinely new work that the others do not require. If the only goal is Group 2 points, a beginner language with a familiar alphabet is the lower-risk choice and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

There are good reasons to choose Arabic anyway. A student who intends to study or work in the Gulf gains something a Spanish grade does not give them. Dubai supplies constant incidental exposure, which keeps motivation alive in a way a classroom-only language cannot. And for a family planning a long stay in the region, functional Arabic has a value that sits outside the Diploma score entirely. Those are real arguments, and a student who holds one of them tends to work through the script phase rather than giving up in it.

The decision needs to be made early, because a Group 2 change after the first term of Year 12 is effectively a restart. If the student is wavering, the useful test is three weeks of script work before the course choice is confirmed. A learner who finds the alphabet interesting will be fine. One who finds it unbearable has learned something important cheaply, and nobody should be discouraged from saying so. We would rather tell a family that beginner Spanish is the safer route than sell two years of lessons into a course the student resents.

sections.heading: Living in Dubai while learning Arabic from zero
paragraphs: Dubai gives a beginner something no textbook does: a reason to read. Street signs, metro announcements, shop fronts, menus and government forms are all bilingual, so a learner who has finished the alphabet starts decoding the environment within weeks. That early success matters disproportionately, because the script phase is where most beginners quit. A tutor who sets reading tasks drawn from the student's own neighbourhood converts the city into practice material at no cost.

The limitation is the variety. Nearly all spoken Arabic a student hears in Dubai is dialect, mostly Gulf, Egyptian or Levantine, while the course assesses Modern Standard Arabic. A beginner who learns their listening from the street will mishear the examination recordings, because negation, question forms, vocabulary and verb endings all differ. The sensible split is to let the environment build reading confidence and motivation while keeping formal listening practice on standard-variety audio from the start, and to name the difference out loud so the student is not confused by it.

Season matters too. The Dubai academic year runs from late August or early September, with a long winter break, a spring break, and reduced hours during Ramadan when many families prefer post-Iftar session times. Summer is a genuine opportunity for a beginner, since six weeks of script and vocabulary work between Year 12 and Year 13 produces more progress than the same hours spread across a busy term. Families who plan that block in advance rather than in July tend to get the slot they want.

sections.heading: Finding a beginner Arabic teacher in Dubai, and what the market charges
paragraphs: Teaching Arabic to a fluent speaker and teaching it to someone who cannot read the alphabet are different jobs, and the second is rarer. Plenty of people in Dubai can speak Arabic beautifully and have never taught a letter shape to a sixteen-year-old. A beginner needs someone who sequences the script, teaches handwriting as a timed skill, works in Modern Standard Arabic rather than drifting into dialect, and plans against twenty prescribed topics rather than a textbook's running order. Within one community, the number of people who fit is very small.

Published Dubai rates give a sense of the market, though they are other providers' figures rather than ours. Budget online tutoring is advertised from around AED 45 to 150 an hour, qualified subject tutors online at roughly AED 150 to 300, in-home visits at AED 180 to 500 once travel is priced in, IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 or more, and premium examiner-led providers up to AED 650. Monthly packages appear at around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for in-home blocks. Those come from the providers' own pages and from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table.

IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is something we offer only in India. Dubai lessons are one-to-one over live video, which for beginner Arabic is close to ideal. Letter formation is demonstrated on a shared screen where the student sees the stroke order clearly rather than upside down across a table. Writing is annotated live. Audio is played at controlled volume and replayed. And the tutor is chosen for being able to take a student from the alphabet to a timed paper, which is the only criterion that matters here.

process.title: Confirm eligibility before anything else
process.description: Ask the Diploma coordinator in writing whether your child qualifies for ab initio given their Arabic record, and when the Group 2 change deadline falls. Tuition planned around a course the school will not allow is wasted. If the answer is no, the conversation becomes an Arabic B conversation and the teaching plan changes completely.

process.title: A free 45-minute trial starting with the alphabet
process.description: The trial is free, runs 45 minutes, and takes no card details. For a genuine beginner it starts with letter shapes and a short dictation, which tells us more in ten minutes than any discussion of prior study. You receive a written note on starting point, the realistic script timeline, and whether the two-year plan is comfortable or tight.

process.title: Front-load the script, then plan the twenty topics
process.description: The term plan compresses the writing system into the first block, then maps the twenty prescribed topics across the remaining terms in the order the school teaches them. Each topic gets a vocabulary core, three or four structures and one short written task at the real length, so coverage is visible rather than assumed.

process.title: Weekly sessions with timed work between them
process.description: Short tasks are set between lessons, written to time, and marked before the session that discusses them. Handwriting speed is tracked explicitly because it limits three of the four components. The running record shows which of the twenty topics are secure, which saves the final term from being spread thinly across all of them.

process.title: Protect the oral window and the summer block
process.description: Two dates drive the plan: the school's internal oral recording window and the summer between Year 12 and Year 13. We ask for the first as early as the school will give it and suggest booking the second in spring, because a beginner gains more from six concentrated summer weeks than from any term-time intensive.

whyPoints.title: Tutors who teach the script, not just the language
whyPoints.description: Taking a student from no alphabet to a timed written paper in two years is a specific skill. Letter sequencing by shape family, joining practice, unvowelled reading and handwriting speed are taught deliberately rather than assumed, because a learner who is still drawing letters in Year 13 cannot finish Paper 1 whatever their vocabulary.

whyPoints.title: Planning against the twenty prescribed topics
whyPoints.description: The examinable content is a finite list, which is the biggest advantage ab initio offers. Lessons are planned against those twenty topics with a vocabulary core and a few reliable structures for each, and a running record of which are secure. General beginners' textbooks do not do this, and the gap shows up in Paper 1.

whyPoints.title: Honest about whether Arabic is the right choice
whyPoints.description: Arabic is harder than beginner Spanish or French for a student used to the Latin alphabet, and we say so before the course is confirmed. Three weeks of script work is a cheap test. A family that chooses Arabic knowing the trade-off tends to finish the course; one sold on it as the easy option often does not.

whyPoints.title: The right pool rather than the nearest tutor
whyPoints.description: People who can teach Arabic from zero to an examined Standard Level are rare in any one Dubai community. Teaching over live video means the match is made on that ability instead of on driving distance, which for a subject with this few specialists is the difference between a real teacher and an available one.

whyPoints.title: Listening started early, because it will not cram
whyPoints.description: Paper 2 carries half the grade and comprehension of spoken Arabic develops over months. Short weekly listening tasks begin in the first term rather than in the final one, graded upward from slow standard-variety audio, with the dialect and standard distinction named explicitly so street Arabic does not confuse the examination material.

whyPoints.title: Sessions that fit a Dubai term
whyPoints.description: Slots are timed to Gulf Standard Time around school finish times and co-curricular fixtures, shift to post-Iftar during Ramadan, and can be booked as a summer block between the Diploma years. No travel sits between consecutive bookings, so a sibling in a different year group can be taught straight afterwards.

faqs.question: Is Arabic ab initio an easier option than Arabic B for a Dubai student?
faqs.answer: It is a lower level with a narrower syllabus, so in that sense yes. It is not an easy course. A student starting from zero has to learn a new writing system, build vocabulary across twenty prescribed topics, and sit a listening paper in a language they did not speak two years earlier. Compared with Arabic B it has shorter written tasks, no literary works and no Higher Level option. Compared with beginner Spanish or French it is harder for a Latin-alphabet speaker, because the script is genuine extra work.

faqs.question: My child has had school Arabic in Dubai since Year 1. Can they still take ab initio?
faqs.answer: Usually not. The course is restricted to students with little or no previous experience of the language, and schools apply that rule even when a student's marks are poor and their confidence lower. KHDA requires Arabic in every Dubai private school whatever the licensed curriculum, so almost every child educated in the emirate carries a long record of Arabic study. Ask the Diploma coordinator what evidence the school uses and whether a transfer from outside the UAE is treated differently, and get the answer before planning a Group 2 choice around it.

faqs.question: How long does it take to learn the Arabic alphabet well enough for the course?
faqs.answer: With weekly one-to-one work and daily short practice, a motivated sixteen-year-old reaches legible writing of dictated words and confident reading of short vowelled text in roughly a term. Reading unvowelled text at speed takes longer, usually into the second term, and handwriting fast enough to finish two timed tasks develops across the first year. Front-loading the script matters because every other part of the course depends on it: a student still forming letters slowly in Year 13 cannot complete Paper 1 however much vocabulary they have acquired.

faqs.question: What are the twenty prescribed topics in Arabic ab initio?
faqs.answer: Four topics sit under each of the five Group 2 themes. Identities covers personal attributes, personal relationships, eating and drinking, and physical well-being. Experiences covers daily routine, leisure, holidays, and festivals and celebrations. Human ingenuity covers transport, entertainment, media and technology. Social organisation covers neighbourhood, education, the workplace and social issues. Sharing the planet covers climate, physical geography, the environment and global issues. That finite list is the course's great advantage over Arabic B, where any topic within a theme may appear in an examination.

faqs.question: How long should each Paper 1 task be in Arabic ab initio?
faqs.answer: Each of the two tasks sits in the region of 70 to 150 words, and both have to be completed inside the paper's one hour. Practising at that real length matters more than most students expect. Learners who draft long answers in lessons routinely write over-length first tasks and unfinished second ones in the examination. Each task also names a text type, which is marked, so a message written as general prose loses marks the Arabic itself did not deserve to lose. Short tasks leave no room to recover from a misread instruction.

faqs.question: What is the ab initio individual oral based on?
faqs.answer: A visual stimulus drawn from the prescribed topics. The student prepares under supervision, presents on the image, answers follow-up questions about it, and then moves into a wider conversation. It is marked by the school and externally moderated, and carries a quarter of the grade. Criteria cover language, the message in response to the stimulus, the message in the conversation, and interactive skills. The commonest beginner mistake is giving short, accurate answers: the interactive criterion rewards extending each answer, so teaching one extra sentence every time earns more than extra vocabulary.

faqs.question: Can my child learn to read Arabic properly over video lessons?
faqs.answer: Letter formation is one of the things video does better than a table. The tutor demonstrates stroke order on a shared screen where the student sees it the right way up rather than upside down or mirrored, writing is annotated live, and the same model can be replayed afterwards. Dictation works identically. Reading practice uses shared text at whatever size suits the student. The part that needs deliberate attention is paper handwriting, which we set between sessions and review as photographed work, because speed on paper is what the examination tests.

faqs.question: Does living in Dubai help a beginner learning Arabic?
faqs.answer: It helps a great deal with motivation and reading. Signage, metro announcements, menus and forms are bilingual, so a student who has finished the alphabet starts decoding their own neighbourhood within weeks, and that early success carries them through the hardest phase. It helps less with listening than families expect, because almost all spoken Arabic heard in Dubai is dialect while the examination uses Modern Standard Arabic. The sensible approach is to use the city for reading and motivation and keep formal listening practice on standard-variety audio from the start.

faqs.question: Should we choose Arabic or Spanish for a beginner language in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: If the only goal is a Group 2 grade with the least risk, a beginner language using the Latin alphabet is the safer choice, because the script is real additional work that Spanish does not require. Arabic earns its place for a different reason: a student planning to study or work in the Gulf gains something lasting, and Dubai supplies constant exposure that keeps the language alive. A fair test is three weeks of script work before the course is confirmed. A student who finds the alphabet interesting will finish the course.

faqs.question: How many hours a week does a beginner need with a tutor?
faqs.answer: One hour weekly plus short daily practice is the usual pattern, with a second hour added during the script block and again before the oral window. The daily practice matters more than the extra contact hour: fifteen minutes of handwriting and vocabulary six days a week outperforms two hours once. The exception is the summer between Year 12 and Year 13, where a concentrated block of three or four sessions a week produces more progress than any term-time arrangement, because nothing else is competing for the student's attention.

faqs.question: Which Dubai schools offer Arabic ab initio in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: It runs in a number of the emirate's IB Diploma schools, usually as a small class, and availability changes year to year with staffing and demand. Students we support come from schools including Swiss International Scientific School Dubai, Nord Anglia International School Dubai, Repton School Dubai, Greenfield International School, Universal American School Dubai and Dubai International Academy Al Barsha. Schools are named as market context only, with no affiliation implied. Always confirm with the school directly, because a subject offered one year may not run the next if numbers are low.

faqs.question: What does beginner Arabic tuition cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published market rates run from roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour for budget online tutoring, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 180 to 500 for in-home visits once travel is priced in, and AED 200 to 450 or more for IB and IGCSE specialists, with premium providers publishing up to AED 650. Monthly packages appear at around AED 799 for eight online sessions. Those figures come from providers' own published pages and Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table rather than from us; ask about our own rates on the trial call.

faqs.question: Will someone come to our villa in Dubai to teach Arabic?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Dubai lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For beginner Arabic the format is genuinely well suited: stroke order is demonstrated on a shared screen rather than across a table, written work is annotated live, and audio is played at a controlled volume. The larger benefit is that the tutor is selected for being able to teach the script rather than for living nearby.

faqs.question: Is two years enough to go from no Arabic to a Standard Level grade?
faqs.answer: It is enough for a student who starts properly and works consistently, and tight for one who spends the first year on vocabulary without securing the script. The decisive variables are handwriting speed, early listening practice and whether the twenty prescribed topics are covered systematically rather than incidentally. Students who treat the course as a beginners' conversation class and discover the written paper in Year 13 do badly. Students who front-load the alphabet in the first term and then work topic by topic generally arrive in reasonable shape.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with a Group 2 Extended Essay in Arabic at this level?
faqs.answer: An Extended Essay written in Arabic is not realistic for an ab initio student, because the language demands sit well above Standard Level beginner work, and schools rarely permit it. What a tutor can do is support an Extended Essay in another subject that draws on Arabic sources in translation, or coach the research and argument skills the essay needs. In all cases the work must be the student's own: a tutor teaches method, questions the argument and gives feedback on drafts, and never supplies text for submission.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-online-tuto.closingHeading: Settle eligibility, then start with the alphabet
dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-online-tuto.closingBody: Two things decide whether beginner Arabic works for your child, and neither of them is the tutor. The first is whether the school will allow the course given your child's Arabic record, which is a question for the Diploma coordinator this week rather than next term. The second is whether the script phase holds their interest, which three weeks of lessons will answer honestly. Send the school name, the year group and what Arabic your child has had, and the free 45-minute trial will start with letter shapes and a short dictation. No card details are taken, and if beginner Spanish is the better route we will say so.

intro.heading: The eligibility question comes before everything else
paragraphs: Arabic ab initio is a Standard Level course for students with no previous experience of learning Arabic. That restriction is not a formality. It exists because the course starts at the alphabet and because a student with three or four years of school Arabic behind them would be competing against genuine beginners. Schools are expected to place students honestly, and a school that enters an experienced learner into ab initio is exposing that candidate rather than helping them.

This is where Dubai differs from almost every other city in which the course is taught. KHDA guidance requires Arabic in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with non-Arab students taught Arabic as an additional language in classes organised separately from the first-language stream. A child who joined a Dubai school in Year 3 and is now in Year 11 has had timetabled Arabic for most of a decade. That student is not an ab initio candidate, whatever their current level, and the honest route for them is Arabic B.

So the realistic Dubai ab initio cohort is narrow: students who arrived in the UAE recently, students who came from a school system with no Arabic provision, and students whose previous schooling was outside the Gulf. Those students are frequently in a hurry, because they are starting a language from nothing with eighteen months before the papers and five other subjects running. That is a real and solvable problem, and it is the one this page is about.

What a beginner actually struggles with is not what parents expect. Grammar is rarely the obstacle. The obstacle is script: twenty-eight letters with different forms depending on position, short vowels that are usually omitted from printed text, and a reading direction that has to become automatic before anything else can be learned efficiently. A student who is still decoding letter by letter in Year 13 cannot do the reading paper at speed, cannot skim a stimulus, and cannot build the vocabulary memory the course assumes.

The second obstacle is the prescribed vocabulary and the functional language around the five themes. Ab initio is assessed on a defined range rather than on open-ended expression, which is good news for a beginner: the territory is finite. A student who works through it systematically, with handwriting and listening practised daily rather than weekly, can reach a solid Standard Level performance from nothing in two years. A student who treats it as a conversation class will not.

IB Gram teaches Arabic ab initio as one-to-one lessons over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time so a session fits after a Dubai school day. We do not offer home visits in the UAE - sending a tutor to an address is a service we run only in India. For a beginner course that is an advantage rather than a compromise: screen sharing makes letter formation, vocalisation marks and script direction easier to demonstrate than a notebook across a table.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-tutor.programmesIntro: Ab initio sits only in the Diploma, but Dubai students arrive at it from different places, and where they came from decides whether the course is open to them at all. These are the programmes around it and what each one means for eligibility.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic ab initio occupies Group 2, the language-acquisition group, at Standard Level only. Three assessed components: written production, listening and reading comprehension, and an individual oral built from a visual stimulus. The course covers prescribed themes with a defined vocabulary range, which makes it the most finite Group 2 syllabus and the one a disciplined beginner can genuinely complete in two years.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the practical constraint is timetabling rather than content. Schools run ab initio only where enough eligible students exist to justify a class, and in many Dubai schools that number is two or three. Those students are often taught in a combined group with Arabic B, at Arabic B pace, which is the single most common reason a Dubai ab initio candidate needs outside support.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic in the Middle Years Programme is assessed in phases, internally, with Phase 1 covering emergent communication. A student who completed any MYP Arabic phase has previous experience of learning the language, which has a direct bearing on ab initio eligibility at sixteen. Phase 1 or 2 in Year 11 points towards Arabic B rather than towards ab initio.
programmes.countryNote: This is where Dubai families are most often surprised. Arabic taught as an additional language under KHDA's mandatory-subject requirement counts as previous experience even when the child retained very little of it. The honest conversation with the Diploma coordinator is about what the school recorded, not about what the student can currently do.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: Where Arabic ab initio is taken as one of the Diploma courses inside the Career-related Programme, the components and the marking are identical to a full Diploma candidate's. The difference is the surrounding load, which carries a reflective project rather than some of the written coursework, often leaving more weekday time for the daily practice a beginner language needs.
programmes.countryNote: Few Dubai schools are authorised to run the Career-related Programme, and fewer still offer ab initio inside it. A CP student taking Arabic from zero is usually taught in whatever Arabic group the timetable allows, which may be a first-language class. That mismatch needs raising with the school early rather than at mock season.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-tutor.subjectsIntro: Ab initio is one of three Arabic routes in the Diploma, and the right one for a given Dubai student depends on prior study rather than on current ability. These are the courses IB Gram covers around it.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: For students with no previous experience of learning Arabic. Prescribed themes and a defined vocabulary range, written production, listening and reading, and an individual oral from a visual stimulus. Script literacy is taught from the alphabet and is the first thing a tutor should timetable.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The route for students who have studied Arabic before, including anyone who has had Arabic as an additional language in a Dubai school. Wider vocabulary, open-ended text types, and at HL two literary works. The destination for most Dubai students who were hoping for ab initio.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Group 1, for first-language Arabic speakers, taught and examined in Modern Standard Arabic. Named here to complete the picture: a family deciding between routes should know what the top of the ladder looks like before assuming their child is on the bottom rung.

subjects.name: French ab initio
subjects.description: The same course design in a different language, and worth comparing because the script problem does not exist. A beginner in French starts with a familiar alphabet, which is why French ab initio moves faster through the themes than Arabic ab initio does in the same number of hours.

subjects.name: Spanish ab initio
subjects.description: Commonly chosen by Dubai students who want a beginner language with the lightest decoding load. Relevant to an Arabic ab initio decision: if the student has no connection to Arabic and a free choice, the workload comparison is honest information.

subjects.name: Mandarin ab initio
subjects.description: The other ab initio course with a significant script demand, and a useful reference point. Students who manage Mandarin characters usually manage Arabic script, because both reward daily short practice over weekly long sessions.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Often the other language course on an ab initio student's timetable, since a recent arrival to Dubai may be acquiring English at the same time. Two acquisition courses in one Diploma is permitted and heavy, and the planning matters more than the teaching.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The 1,600-word prescribed-title essay and the exhibition. Named here because a new arrival to a Dubai school often needs core support before subject support, and TOK is the core element schools explain least well to mid-year joiners.

subjects.name: MYP Arabic language acquisition
subjects.description: Where a Dubai student's recorded Arabic history usually sits. Checking which phase the school entered your child in matters, because that record is what a Diploma coordinator will use when deciding whether ab initio is open.

regions.name: Jumeirah Islands and Emirates Living
regions.note: Longer-settled families whose children have had Dubai school Arabic since primary, so genuine ab initio cases here are rare. The useful service in this area is usually an eligibility conversation that redirects the family to Arabic B before money is spent.

sections.heading: Who is actually eligible for Arabic ab initio in Dubai
paragraphs: Ab initio courses are designed for students with no previous experience of learning the language. The school decides placement and the school carries the responsibility for getting it right. In most cities that decision is simple, because a student either studied the language or did not. In Dubai it is complicated by a regulatory fact: Arabic is a mandatory subject in every private school in the emirate, so almost every long-term resident student has a recorded Arabic history.

The question a Dubai family should put to the Diploma coordinator is therefore specific. Not 'can my child take ab initio' but 'what Arabic study does the school have on record for my child, and from which year'. That record is what the decision rests on. A student who had Arabic as an additional language from Year 3 to Year 9 has previous experience of learning Arabic even if they cannot currently read a sentence, and entering them into ab initio is a risk to the candidate rather than a shortcut.

The students for whom ab initio is genuinely the right course are a smaller and identifiable group, and the table sets them out. If your child is in the ineligible column, the useful next step is an honest Arabic B plan rather than an argument, because Arabic B from a low base is a workable two-year project and a withdrawn entry at mock season is not.

One more reason to settle this early: the choice interacts with the rest of the timetable. Group 2 cannot be dropped, ab initio exists at Standard Level only, and a student who needs three Higher Level subjects must therefore find all three outside their language. A family who assumes ab initio is available and builds a subject-choice form around it can end up reworking the whole combination in September, with option blocks already closed. Ask the eligibility question in the spring of Year 11, in writing, while there is still room to change the other five subjects.

sections.heading: Why Dubai's mandatory Arabic rules close the door for most residents
paragraphs: Dubai private schools are overseen by KHDA, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Alongside inspection, KHDA sets the requirements for the mandatory UAE subjects, and those requirements are the reason the ab initio door is closed to most Dubai-raised students. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies run in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum.

The rules are specific enough to be checkable. Schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and it is advised that no mandatory subject lesson runs shorter than 25 minutes. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education must hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects.

For an ab initio family the consequence is practical rather than philosophical. Your child has probably had hundreds of hours of timetabled Arabic as an additional language. Whether they retained much of it is a separate question from whether it happened, and placement turns on the second. The more useful thing to take from the rules is that the hours were there and can be built on: a student with eight years of light exposure is not a beginner, and they are also not starting from nothing in Arabic B.

sections.heading: Ab initio, Arabic B or Arabic A: placing a new arrival honestly
paragraphs: A family arriving in Dubai mid-secondary faces a three-way choice that will shape two years of their child's timetable, and schools make it quickly with limited information. The three Arabic routes are genuinely different courses rather than three difficulty settings of one course, and a student can be on the wrong one in either direction. Over-placement produces a predictable collapse in Year 13. Under-placement produces a wasted grade and, for a heritage speaker, boredom.

The useful diagnostic is not conversation. A heritage speaker can hold a fluent exchange in dialect and be unable to read a newspaper headline, which makes them wrong for Arabic A and wrong for ab initio at the same time. The three things worth testing are: can the student read unvocalised printed Arabic at reasonable speed, can they write a paragraph in Modern Standard Arabic, and have they ever studied Arabic formally. Those three answers place a student reliably.

A tutor's role at this stage is diagnostic rather than instructional, and it is the one place where a single paid session is good value. Forty-five minutes with a reading passage, a short written task and a few questions about schooling history produces a recommendation a family can take to the Diploma coordinator. What it cannot do is override the school's decision, which rests on the record the school holds and on its own judgement.

Over-placement is the error with the worse consequences, and it happens for understandable reasons. A new arrival wants to look capable, a parent wants the harder course on the transcript, and a coordinator short of information takes the family's word for the student's level. Eighteen months later the student is sitting a paper written for readers of literary Arabic. Under-placement is recoverable: a student finding Arabic B easy can be stretched inside it. Over-placement in a language course is not recoverable in the time available, which is why the conservative choice is usually the correct one when the evidence is thin.

sections.heading: What ab initio assesses, and why the finite syllabus helps
paragraphs: Ab initio has three assessed components and no written coursework. Written production is examined under timed conditions. Listening and reading comprehension are examined together and carry the largest single share of the grade. The individual oral is built from a visual stimulus, followed by questions, and is recorded and moderated like every other Group 2 oral.

What distinguishes ab initio from Arabic B is the defined range. The course is built on prescribed themes with a specified vocabulary and set of functional structures, which means the territory a student has to cover is finite and knowable. For a beginner with eighteen months, that is the most important fact about the course. It is possible to be systematically thorough in ab initio in a way that is not possible in a course assessed on open-ended expression, and a tutor's first job is to convert the prescribed range into a working schedule.

Treat the weightings below as the shape of the course rather than as a quotation from the current subject guide, and confirm the detail with your child's Diploma coordinator before building a revision timetable on it. The IB revises course structures on a cycle, schools set internal deadlines months ahead of external ones, and the figure that matters for planning is the school's recording window rather than any published external date.

There is a practical corollary of the finite range that beginners exploit too rarely. Because the vocabulary is prescribed, a student can know with confidence when a theme is finished, which is impossible in a course assessed on open expression. That turns revision from an anxious activity into a checklist one. Keep a single cumulative record, mark each item as recognised in reading, understood in listening, and produced in writing, and the three columns show exactly what the next session should be about. Students who maintain that record arrive at mocks knowing where they stand; students who keep separate notebooks per theme never do.

sections.heading: Where beginners lose marks: script before grammar
paragraphs: The marks a Dubai ab initio student loses are rarely lost where their parents expect. Grammar is a small part of the problem. Decoding is most of it. Arabic has twenty-eight letters, each taking a different form depending on whether it stands alone or sits at the start, middle or end of a word, and printed text normally omits the short-vowel marks that tell a reader how to pronounce what they are seeing. A student who has not automated that will read the reading paper at a third of the speed the paper assumes.

The knock-on effects are what make it expensive. Slow decoding means the student cannot skim, so they cannot locate information in a passage and must read every line. In the listening paper, weak letter-sound mapping means words heard in connected speech are not recognised even when they are known in writing. In the oral, attention spent on retrieving pronunciation is attention not spent on content. One underlying problem produces four separate symptoms, which is why the symptoms do not respond to being treated individually.

The remedy is unfashionable: daily handwriting practice, reading aloud in every session however slow, and letter-form drills until the forms are automatic. Ten to fifteen minutes a day for six weeks does more than an hour a week for six months, because motor memory responds to frequency. Families who want to see progress fast should ask any prospective tutor what their plan for script literacy is, and be wary of a plan that starts with vocabulary lists.
