sections.heading: The individual oral from a visual stimulus
paragraphs: The ab initio individual oral starts from a visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed themes. The student describes it, then answers the teacher's questions, and the recording is moderated. For a beginner this is the component with the widest gap between what is achievable and what students typically achieve, because the skill being tested is sustaining simple language rather than producing complex language.

The failure pattern is consistent. A student describes the image in three sentences, exhausts the vocabulary they have for it, and then produces single-word answers to the questions. The marks were available for continuing: naming what is in the picture, saying where it is, saying what the people are doing, saying what they might be thinking, comparing it with something familiar. That sequence is formulaic and can be practised on any image, which is exactly why it should be. A student with a rehearsed sequence does not run dry at sentence three.

Rehearsal needs unseen material, which is the practical argument for working with a tutor rather than with a parent or alone. A tutor can supply a fresh stimulus every session, record the attempt, play it back, and ask the questions a teacher would ask. Ten rehearsals turns the oral from an ordeal into a routine. It also exposes pronunciation errors that have become fossilised, which a student practising alone will reinforce rather than correct.

The playback is the part students resist and the part that does the work. Hearing yourself pause for four seconds, hearing the same filler word nine times, hearing an answer that stopped after six words - none of that is visible from the inside, and all of it is obvious on a recording. A tutor pointing it out is easy to discount; a recording is not. Two sessions of playback usually change a student's pacing more than a term of being told to slow down and keep going, and the recording habit also removes the surprise of being recorded on the day that counts.

sections.heading: Eighteen months from zero: a term-by-term plan
paragraphs: A student starting Arabic from nothing in September of Year 12 has about eighteen months of usable time before the final components. That is enough, and it is only enough if the sequence is right. The commonest planning error is to start with themes and vocabulary, because that feels like progress, and to leave script literacy to improve by exposure. It does not improve by exposure quickly enough, and the whole schedule then runs at decoding speed.

The sequence that works puts the alphabet first and accepts six weeks of apparently slow progress to buy speed for the following seventeen months. Theme coverage then runs continuously, written production starts immediately and never stops, listening becomes daily, and oral rehearsal concentrates in the term before the recording. Reading aloud happens in every session from the first week to the last, which is the single habit most correlated with a comfortable Year 13 in this subject.

The plan below is counted in terms rather than in dates, deliberately. IB session and results dates are set by the IB and we do not publish them here: no date in this project has been confirmed against ibo.org, which blocks automated checking, so confirm every deadline with your child's Diploma coordinator. What matters more for planning anyway is the school's internal recording and submission windows, which sit well before the external ones and differ between Dubai schools.

Two UAE calendar features belong in the plan rather than beside it. The long summer break falls between Year 12 and Year 13, exactly where a beginner most needs consolidation, and it is the one stretch of the plan with no competing subjects: three short sessions a week through July and August do more for decoding speed than the whole of the following term. And during Ramadan most Dubai families move sessions to after iftar and keep the weekly rhythm, which matters for a beginner language because a month's gap in daily practice undoes more than a month's progress.

sections.heading: Academic honesty, and what a tutor may do for a beginner
paragraphs: Ab initio carries no written coursework, which narrows the academic-honesty question but does not remove it. The individual oral is recorded and moderated by the IB, and a scripted oral delivered from memory is a misrepresentation of the student's ability in exactly the way the component is designed to detect. A tutor who writes an oral for a student to learn by heart is not helping them; they are building a performance that collapses in the question phase and may expose the candidate.

The line in practice is clear enough to state. A tutor may teach the alphabet and the prescribed vocabulary, supply unseen stimuli, rehearse the oral and ask examiner-style questions, mark written tasks against the criteria, correct pronunciation, and set reading and listening. A tutor may not script an oral for memorisation, write a student's written task, or sit beside a student during an assessed recording. Where a student also takes a Group 2 Extended Essay, note that an ab initio language is not normally an eligible subject for it; confirm with the coordinator rather than assuming.

The materials point applies here too. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and vocabulary lists published by the IB belong to the IB and are licensed to schools. IB Gram links to official pages rather than redistributing files, and anything on this page about course structure should be checked against the current subject guide your child's school holds. A provider offering to send you a pack of IB documents is offering something they are not entitled to supply.

process.title: Start with the eligibility question
process.description: Tell us what Arabic your child has studied, from which year, and in which school system. If the answer suggests they are not an ab initio candidate, we will say so before anything is booked. An eligibility conversation that redirects a family to Arabic B is a better outcome than a wasted term.

process.title: Take the free trial as a diagnostic
process.description: Forty-five minutes, one per family, no card details taken. A reading passage, a short written attempt and a few questions about schooling history. That produces a recommendation on route and a plan for script literacy, both of which you can take to your child's Diploma coordinator.

process.title: Fix the sequence before the content
process.description: Script first, for six weeks, then themes continuously with written production running throughout. Families frequently want to start with vocabulary because it feels productive. Agreeing the sequence at the outset prevents the conversation recurring every month.

process.title: Set the daily habit, not just the session
process.description: Beginner languages respond to frequency. Fifteen minutes of handwriting and five minutes of reading aloud, daily, does more than the weekly session does. The session's job is to correct and extend what the daily practice built, and without the daily practice there is little to correct.

process.title: Audit theme coverage at the end of each term
process.description: The prescribed range is finite, so coverage can be checked rather than estimated. A termly audit against the cumulative vocabulary record finds the gaps while there is time to close them, instead of a mock finding them in Year 13.

whyPoints.title: Eligibility checked before money changes hands
whyPoints.description: Most Dubai families who search for ab initio support have a child who is not eligible for the course, because Arabic is mandatory in every Dubai private school. We tell you that at the enquiry stage rather than after a term of lessons aimed at the wrong syllabus.

whyPoints.title: Script literacy taught as a subject, not assumed
whyPoints.description: Decoding unvocalised Arabic at speed is the obstacle that produces four separate symptoms across reading, listening and the oral. It is taught explicitly from the alphabet, with daily handwriting, rather than left to improve by exposure.

whyPoints.title: Online suits a beginner script course
whyPoints.description: Screen sharing demonstrates letter forms, joining and vocalisation marks more clearly than a notebook passed across a table, and the session can be recorded for review. IB Gram makes no UAE home visits; that is a service we run only in India.

whyPoints.title: A finite syllabus turned into a schedule
whyPoints.description: Ab initio's prescribed range is its biggest advantage for a student in a hurry. We convert it into a term-by-term plan with coverage audited at the end of each term, so gaps are found while there is still time to close them.

whyPoints.title: Honest about the oral
whyPoints.description: Rehearsal with unseen stimuli and playback, not a script to memorise. Scripted orals fall apart in the question phase and misrepresent a candidate's ability in a recording that goes to the IB for moderation.

whyPoints.title: No claimed approvals or UAE premises
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, Ministry of Education, IB or Cambridge approval or partnership and operates no UAE office. We cite what regulators publish and explain what it means, which is a different thing from implying an endorsement.

faqs.question: Can my child take Arabic ab initio if they have had Arabic lessons at their Dubai school?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Ab initio is designed for students with no previous experience of learning the language, and Arabic is a mandatory subject in every Dubai private school, so a long-term resident student will have a recorded Arabic history even if they retained very little. The decision rests with the school and on the record it holds. Ask the Diploma coordinator what Arabic study is recorded for your child and from which year, and ask for any placement decision in writing. The honest alternative for most Dubai students is Arabic B at Standard Level.

faqs.question: Is Arabic ab initio available at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: No. Ab initio courses are offered at Standard Level only, across every language that has one. A student who wants a Higher Level language in Group 2 needs a Language B course, which assumes prior study and a wider vocabulary range. For a Diploma candidate choosing three Higher Level subjects, that means the Higher Level choices have to come from elsewhere on the timetable. Confirm the current structure with your child's Diploma coordinator, because the Higher Level combination affects university prerequisites in ways a subject choice form does not explain.

faqs.question: What is the hardest part of Arabic for a complete beginner in Year 12?
faqs.answer: Reading. Arabic has twenty-eight letters, each taking a different shape depending on its position in the word, and printed text usually omits the short-vowel marks that tell a reader how to pronounce it. Until decoding is automatic, every other skill runs at decoding speed: the student cannot skim a reading passage, cannot recognise known words in connected speech, and spends attention in the oral on pronunciation rather than content. Grammar, which parents expect to be the obstacle, is a much smaller part of the problem.

faqs.question: How much daily practice does Arabic ab initio actually need?
faqs.answer: Fifteen minutes of handwriting and five minutes of reading aloud, every day, through the first six weeks and then continuing at a lower intensity. Motor memory and letter-sound mapping respond to frequency rather than to session length, so twenty minutes daily outperforms a single long weekly session by a wide margin. The weekly tutored session's job is to correct and extend what the daily practice has built. Without the daily practice there is little for the session to work on and progress stalls regardless of the tutor.

faqs.question: My child is a heritage speaker who never studied Arabic formally. Which route fits?
faqs.answer: Usually Arabic B rather than ab initio, even without formal study, because ab initio is not designed for a student with substantial spoken exposure. A heritage speaker can hold a fluent exchange in dialect and be unable to read a headline, which makes them wrong for Arabic A as well. The three things worth testing are whether they can read unvocalised printed Arabic at speed, whether they can write a paragraph in Modern Standard Arabic, and what the school has on record. Schools treat home-language exposure differently, so ask yours directly.

faqs.question: What does the ab initio individual oral involve?
faqs.answer: The student is given a visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed themes, describes it, and then answers the teacher's questions. The recording is moderated by the IB. Beginners typically describe the image in three sentences, run out of language, and give single-word answers in the question phase, which is exactly where the marks sit. A rehearsed sequence - name what is there, say where it is, say what people are doing, speculate, compare - works on any image and stops a student drying up. Ten rehearsals with playback is the realistic preparation.

faqs.question: Can a tutor write my child's oral for them to learn by heart?
faqs.answer: No, and a tutor who offers to is doing the student harm. The oral is recorded and sent to the IB for moderation, and a memorised script collapses the moment the teacher asks a question outside it, which is the part of the component designed to test real ability. It is also a misrepresentation of the candidate's work. What a tutor can legitimately do is supply unseen stimuli, rehearse, record, play back, correct pronunciation, and ask the questions a teacher would ask until the student can handle them unprepared.

faqs.question: Can my child submit an Extended Essay in Arabic if they are taking ab initio?
faqs.answer: Normally not. A Group 2 Extended Essay is written in a Language B language rather than an ab initio one, because the essay demands a level of written expression the ab initio range does not cover. Students in this position usually base the Extended Essay on another subject entirely, which is a perfectly ordinary choice and often a better one. Confirm the current position with your child's Diploma coordinator before any research starts, because an essay begun in the wrong subject costs a term of work.

faqs.question: Our school does not run an ab initio group. What are the options?
faqs.answer: Three, and they should be weighed in this order. First, ask whether the school will enter the student for ab initio while teaching them inside the Arabic B group, which is common and workable with outside support. Second, ask whether a different ab initio language is timetabled, since Spanish and French ab initio carry no script-learning load and move faster from zero. Third, consider Arabic B at Standard Level with a two-year plan. The school's answer to the first question usually decides the other two.

faqs.question: Is eighteen months enough to go from no Arabic to a solid Standard Level grade?
faqs.answer: It is enough, provided the sequence is right and the daily practice happens. The prescribed vocabulary range is finite, which is the single most useful feature of this course for a student in a hurry: the territory can be covered systematically rather than endlessly. What makes eighteen months insufficient is starting with themes and leaving script literacy to improve by exposure, because the whole schedule then runs at decoding speed. No tutor can promise a particular grade, but the plan is a realistic one and the course is designed for it.

faqs.question: Why is online delivery suitable for teaching a script from scratch?
faqs.answer: Because the thing being demonstrated is small, precise and best seen magnified. Letter forms in each position, how letters join, where the vocalisation marks sit and why they disappear in printed text all show more clearly on a shared screen than in a notebook across a table, and the session can be recorded so the student can rewatch a letter being formed. IB Gram delivers one-to-one lessons over live video and makes no home visits in the UAE; sending a tutor to an address is a service we run only in India.

faqs.question: How many prescribed themes does the ab initio course cover?
faqs.answer: Five, and they are the same five that frame every Group 2 course: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. What makes ab initio different is that the vocabulary and functional language within each theme are prescribed rather than open-ended, so coverage can be audited. A termly check of a single cumulative vocabulary record against the prescribed range finds gaps while there is time to close them, which is a discipline very few beginner students maintain without someone asking for it.

faqs.question: Does ab initio cost less to support than Arabic B?
faqs.answer: Usually a little, because the vocabulary range is narrower and there are no literary works to prepare, so the tutor's unpaid preparation load is lighter. Market rates for a qualified subject tutor online in Dubai run roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour on published figures, with IB specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. Those are market numbers from providers' own pages and the 2026 Bestimate rate table, not ours. What drives total cost in ab initio is session frequency in the first six weeks rather than the hourly figure.

faqs.question: Do private Arabic tutors working with Dubai students need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Any individual providing private tuition in the UAE needs a private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years through MoHRE's smart app, website and e-services system. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so treat any specific amount circulating online as unverified.

faqs.question: What if no Arabic ab initio specialist is free when we need one?
faqs.answer: You get told, with a date, rather than matched to a general Arabic teacher. Teaching a non-Arabic speaker to read unvocalised text in two years is a specific skill and the pool is small, because most Arabic tutors work with students who can already read. The options are a different slot with the right specialist, a tutor outside the UAE working to Gulf Standard Time, or a short wait. Delivery is online in every case, so geography is never the constraint; the constraint is how few people teach Arabic from the alphabet upwards.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-tutor.closingHeading: Check eligibility first, then start with the alphabet
dubai/ib-dp-arabic-ab-initio-tutor.closingBody: Two things decide whether Arabic ab initio works for a Dubai student: whether the course is actually open to them, and whether script literacy is taught before anything else. The trial lesson answers both. Forty-five minutes, free, one per family, no card details taken, with a reading attempt and a few questions about schooling history, produces a recommendation you can take to your child's Diploma coordinator. If the answer is that Arabic B is the right route, we will say so. Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach Arabic B at Diploma level, SL and HL, to students across Dubai's IB, British and American schools. They teach the components separately, because a student weak in listening and strong in writing needs two different plans, not one general Arabic class.

intro.heading: Arabic B is three skills wearing one subject name
paragraphs: Arabic B is a language acquisition course, and the Diploma assesses it in three pieces that have almost nothing in common. Paper 1 is a single piece of writing in a specified text type, marked out of 30 on language, message and conceptual understanding. Paper 2 is listening and reading comprehension, worth half the subject. The individual oral is a recorded conversation, also out of 30, built from a visual stimulus at Standard Level and from a literary extract at Higher Level. A student can be comfortable in one and lost in another, and a report that says Arabic B grade 4 hides which.

That is the first thing we establish. Not how good is your child at Arabic, which is unanswerable, but which of the three components is producing the low number. The answer is usually visible on a marked mock within twenty minutes. Writing that scores well on language and badly on conceptual understanding means the student can write Arabic but ignored the text type. Reading that scores and listening that does not means the gap is audio processing speed, which responds to a specific and slightly tedious drill.

Dubai adds a complication at the other end of the range. Arabic B here is taken by three very different students: a non-Arab expatriate who has studied Arabic since primary as the school's mandatory provision, a heritage speaker who talks at home and reads slowly, and a late arrival who joined a Dubai school at fourteen with no Arabic at all. All three sit the same paper. The heritage speaker is the one most likely to be in the wrong course entirely, and we will say so if the evidence points that way.

What a session fixes is narrower than families expect and more useful. A session can fix text type conventions, because those are a finite list learned in a fortnight. It can fix the structure of a Paper 1 response, the handling of a visual stimulus, the order of a reading paper, and the grammar errors that recur on a specific student's work. It cannot manufacture vocabulary breadth in six weeks, and anyone promising that is selling something. We say which of your child's problems is in which category before you commit to a term.

Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. The format is not incidental to Arabic B: listening practice needs clean shared audio with the ability to stop, replay a three-second span and transcribe it, and that is easier on a screen share than across a dining table with a phone speaker. The oral is rehearsed with the recording played back to the student so they mark their own interactive skills before anyone else does.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic B at Diploma level sits on top of whatever Arabic a Dubai school provided before 16, and that varies enormously between curricula. These notes describe what each prior stage tends to leave missing by the time Paper 1 arrives.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic B fills the Group 2 language acquisition slot at SL or HL. Five prescribed themes frame the course: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. HL adds two literary works and a longer Paper 1 and listening component. Assessment is Paper 1 writing, Paper 2 listening and reading, and an internally assessed individual oral.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai DP cohorts take Arabic B for reasons that have nothing to do with language interest: it is the familiar option after years of mandatory school Arabic, and it is often the only Group 2 language the timetable offers alongside French. That means a wide spread of starting points in one room, which is exactly the condition one-to-one work is for.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic appears as Language Acquisition across six phases, assessed on four criteria covering listening, reading, speaking and writing. A student's phase at the end of MYP5 is the best single predictor of whether Arabic B SL or HL is realistic, and it is a number most parents have never been shown.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP phase to Arabic B step is where Dubai students lose confidence. MYP Language Acquisition rewards communication; Arabic B Paper 1 rewards producing a named text type for a named audience with the right register. A student at a comfortable MYP phase 4 can open DP1 and score in single figures on conceptual understanding without their Arabic having got worse.

programmes.name: IGCSE Arabic as a foreign language
programmes.description: Many Dubai students arrive at Arabic B from an IGCSE Arabic course rather than from MYP. The IGCSE route trains tight, short, accurate answers and controlled writing tasks. It trains comparatively little extended writing and almost no conceptual framing of audience and purpose.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum students in Dubai moving from IGCSE Arabic into Arabic B HL are the group we most often see underestimate Paper 1. Their accuracy is usually fine. Their problem is that an IGCSE writing task and an Arabic B text type task look similar and are marked on different things.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: A plan for Arabic B names components and error classes rather than topics. These are the units of work we actually build sessions around, with the marks attached so the priority order is visible.

subjects.name: Paper 1 text type production
subjects.levels: SL 1 h 15 min - HL 1 h 30 min
subjects.description: One task chosen from three, each tied to a prescribed theme and a named text type: blog, email, article, speech, report, review, proposal, diary, interview. Marked out of 30. The task choice is itself a skill, and students routinely pick the theme they like over the text type they can produce.

subjects.name: Conceptual understanding, criterion C
subjects.description: Six marks for audience, purpose, context and register being right for the text type requested. The cheapest marks on the paper and the most completely lost. A student who writes a well-argued essay when a speech was asked for keeps the language marks and loses this criterion outright.

subjects.name: Paper 2 listening comprehension
subjects.description: Recorded passages in Modern Standard Arabic at natural speed, answered under time. The component nobody practises, because practising it alone is unpleasant. Dubai students who hear dialect daily and fusha only in class find the audio register unfamiliar rather than the vocabulary difficult.

subjects.name: Paper 2 reading comprehension
subjects.description: Authentic written texts with comprehension questions, where the marks turn on locating and lifting precisely rather than on understanding broadly. Students lose marks by answering in their own words when the question wanted the text's, or by over-answering and burying the required detail.

subjects.name: Individual oral at SL: the visual stimulus
subjects.description: The student presents a photograph linked to one of the five themes, then holds a conversation on it, then discusses at least one further theme. Marked on language, message and interactive skills. Describing the photograph instead of using it to make a point is the most common way to cap the message marks.

subjects.name: Individual oral at HL: the literary extract
subjects.description: The HL oral starts from an extract from one of the two literary works studied rather than from an image. Students who treated the literary works as background reading arrive with nothing to say about the extract, and the discussion that follows has no foundation to build on.

subjects.name: Recurring written accuracy errors
subjects.description: Hamza placement, taa marbuta against haa, alif maqsura, broken plurals, idafa constructions and the reverse agreement of numbers three to ten. Finite, listable, and worth real marks under the language criterion. We build the list from the student's own scripts rather than from a textbook chapter.

subjects.name: Verb forms and tense control
subjects.description: The derived verb patterns and the weak verbs are where fluent-sounding writing comes apart on the page. Most Arabic B candidates can use the perfect and imperfect and avoid everything else, which flattens the language criterion however rich the vocabulary is.

subjects.name: Dialect interference for heritage speakers
subjects.description: A student who speaks Levantine or Egyptian Arabic at home writes those structures without noticing. Marking it as inaccuracy is unhelpful; identifying their particular substitutions is a fortnight of work and visible in the next marked piece.

subjects.name: Handwriting speed and legibility under time
subjects.description: Arabic script written at pace degrades, and an unreadable word earns nothing regardless of whether it was correct. Students whose coursework is strong and whose mocks are weak often have a stamina and legibility problem rather than a knowledge one.

sections.heading: Arabic B at a glance: what each component is worth
paragraphs: Arabic B is assessed in three components with fixed weightings, and knowing them changes where revision effort goes. Paper 1 writing carries 25%. Paper 2, which is listening and reading taken together, carries 50%. The internally assessed individual oral carries the remaining 25%. The implication is uncomfortable for most students: half the grade sits in the one component that cannot be revised by writing practice, and listening is the half of that half which nobody enjoys doing alone.

Durations differ by level and matter for practice planning. Paper 1 is an hour and a quarter at SL and an hour and a half at HL. The listening component is forty-five minutes at SL and an hour at HL; reading is an hour at both. The oral is fifteen minutes, with preparation time before it. Higher Level additionally requires two literary works, which exist on the course for one purpose: they supply the extract the HL oral starts from.

What follows from the table is a priority order, and it is usually not the order a student would choose. If Paper 2 is weak, Paper 2 is the work, however much more satisfying it is to polish an essay. If conceptual understanding is the only low criterion on Paper 1, that is six marks available for about two weeks of attention to text type conventions. We set the order from the marked evidence in the first session and write it down so it can be checked against later.

sections.heading: The five themes, and why they are not topics
paragraphs: Arabic B runs on five prescribed themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. Students treat them as a vocabulary syllabus, which is a reasonable misreading and costs marks. The themes are not lists of words to memorise. They are the contexts a Paper 1 task will be set in and the conversation territory the oral will move through, which means the useful preparation is being able to say something with a position in each of them.

In practice that distinction shows up in the message criterion. A student with strong theme vocabulary can produce four paragraphs about technology containing no argument, and will score on language and not on message. A student with narrower vocabulary and a clear claim about human ingenuity will often outscore them. Preparing a theme properly means arriving with two or three positions you could defend, not forty nouns.

The Dubai advantage here is real and underused. Every one of the five themes has an immediate local example a student can speak about with specifics: residency and identity in a city where most people are from somewhere else, the physical experience of a summer, desalination and water under sharing the planet, the organisation of a school system running seventeen different curricula. Specific local examples read as genuine content in the oral, and they are the one thing a student has that a textbook does not supply. A candidate who can name the thing they are describing, in Arabic, with a detail attached to it, sounds like someone with something to say rather than someone reciting a theme.

sections.heading: Text type is six marks and the cheapest ones on the paper
paragraphs: Paper 1 names a text type: a blog post, a formal email, a speech to a school assembly, a report, a review, a set of instructions, a proposal, a diary entry, an interview. Six of the thirty marks, under conceptual understanding, go to getting the audience, purpose, context and register right for that text type. Those six marks are available to a student with modest Arabic and are routinely forfeited in full by a strong one who wrote a good essay instead of the thing requested.

The remedy is a short, finite piece of learning, which is why it is the first thing we do with a student whose criterion C marks are low. Each text type has a handful of conventions: how it opens, how it addresses its reader, whether it carries a heading or a sign-off, how formal the register sits, whether it is allowed to use the first person. That is a page of notes per type and about a fortnight of practice to make automatic under time pressure.

There is a second-order gain. Task choice on Paper 1 is itself a decision worth marks, and students make it on theme rather than on text type. A candidate who knows they write a clean formal email and a shapeless speech should choose the email task even if the speech topic appeals more. Deciding that in advance, on the evidence of marked practice, turns three minutes at the start of the paper from a gamble into a plan.

rows: A named adult in an institution

A title, and any sense that the reader is being addressed directly

sections.heading: Where Dubai Arabic B candidates lose marks on paper
paragraphs: The language criterion is twelve of the thirty marks on Paper 1 and twelve on the oral, and it is lost in patterns rather than randomly. After enough marked scripts the same families of error appear: hamza placement, taa marbuta written as haa, alif maqsura confusion, broken plurals avoided by using singulars, idafa constructions built in the wrong order, and the reverse agreement of numbers three to ten getting agreement the usual way round. None of this is mysterious and all of it is listable.

That is the method. Rather than teaching Arabic grammar from the top, we build an error list from the student's own marked work: their recurring items, numbered, usually between twelve and twenty. The student checks their own writing against their own list before it is submitted. The list shortens over a term because items leave it when they stop appearing, and the language criterion marks move with it. It is a dull instrument and it works better than a grammar course.

The second pattern is avoidance, which does not look like an error at all. A student who can only use the perfect and imperfect writes everything in them and never risks a derived form or a passive. The script is accurate and flat, and the language criterion notices range as well as accuracy. Pushing a student to use three structures they currently avoid, and accepting mistakes while they do it, is a short-term mark cost and the only route past a ceiling they have usually been sitting on for two years.

sections.heading: Paper 2: half the grade in the component nobody practises
paragraphs: Listening and reading together are 50% of Arabic B, and they are the components students do least work on, because both are unpleasant to practise alone and neither produces anything to show a parent. Reading at least looks like studying. Listening involves sitting with an audio file failing to understand it, which almost nobody chooses voluntarily. The result is predictable: a cohort whose written Arabic is decent and whose Paper 2 marks are not.

The drill that works is small-span and repetitive. Take three to five minutes of audio. Play ten seconds. Transcribe what was heard, including the gaps. Replay. Fill what can be filled. Replay again, then read the transcript. The student is not practising comprehension at this stage, they are training the ear to segment connected fusha speech, and the comprehension marks follow once segmentation stops being the bottleneck. Twenty minutes, three times a week, beats a full paper on a Sunday.

Reading fails differently. The marks turn on precision rather than understanding: locating the required information and lifting it in the form the question wants. Students lose marks by paraphrasing when the text's own words were needed, by writing three sentences where one was asked for and burying the answer, and by running out of time on the last text because they read everything in order at the same depth. Sorting the question types, and practising each type on its own, converts reading from a comprehension problem into a technique problem.

sections.heading: The individual oral: two different exams with one name
paragraphs: At Standard Level the oral starts from a visual stimulus linked to one of the five themes. At Higher Level it starts from an extract from one of the two literary works studied. Both are fifteen minutes, both are marked out of 30, and both are internally assessed by the school and recorded. In every other respect they are different exams requiring different preparation, and a student who revises for the wrong one has wasted the block.

The SL failure mode is describing the photograph. A student who narrates what is visible for four minutes has produced no message to mark, and the conversation afterwards has nothing to build on. The stimulus is a prompt for a position about the theme, not a picture-description exercise. The preparation that fixes it is cold practice: a new, unseen image every session, three minutes to plan, then speak, with the recording played back and marked by the student before the tutor says anything.

The HL failure mode is treating the literary works as background reading. Two works are studied and most of their function is to supply this extract, so a student who skimmed them has no foothold when a passage appears in front of them. The work that pays is annotating both texts for themes, characters and a few quotable moments, then practising on extracts from them cold. The general conversation afterwards ranges across themes, so one further theme should be prepared with specific examples whichever level is being sat.

sections.heading: Arabic B or Arabic A: the choice heritage speakers get wrong
paragraphs: A sizeable minority of Dubai students sitting Arabic B should be sitting Arabic A. They are heritage speakers: Arabic at home, English at school since Foundation Stage, fluent in conversation and slow in fusha reading. Schools place them in Arabic B because their written Arabic looks weak, and Arabic B is the safer timetable decision. It is also, for a first-language speaker, a course beneath their level, and it closes the bilingual diploma route that two language A courses at grade 3 or above would open.

The test is not fluency. It is reading speed and register control in Modern Standard Arabic. A student who can read an unfamiliar fusha page at reasonable pace and discuss it has the raw material for Arabic A: Literature, even if their writing currently shows dialect interference, because that is correctable. A student who decodes slowly and loses the thread of a paragraph is genuinely better served by Arabic B, where they can score well rather than struggle respectably.

This is worth raising in DP1 while the timetable can still move, and it is worth raising even when the answer is to stay. Where a Dubai school runs no Arabic A class, the IB's school-supported self-taught Literature SL route exists and is usually the parent who raises it, not the school. We will give a view based on a reading diagnostic rather than on an impression, and the view sometimes costs us the Arabic B booking. Your child's DP coordinator makes the decision; our job is to make it an informed one.

sections.heading: What a session fixes, what it does not, and what it costs
paragraphs: Honesty about scope is more useful than enthusiasm. Six weeks of one-to-one Arabic B work will reliably fix text type conventions, Paper 1 structure, visual stimulus handling, reading question technique and a named list of recurring accuracy errors. Six weeks will not build broad vocabulary or fluent listening from a low base, because both are functions of hours of exposure that no tutor can compress. Families who know which of their problems is in which column make better decisions about how much tutoring to buy.

The Dubai market context is worth stating plainly because so few pages do. Published rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table put qualified online subject tutors at roughly AED 150-300 an hour in this city, IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200-450, and in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180-500 with travel priced inside the hour. Those are market figures from October 2026, not an IB Gram price list. We start with a free trial lesson and quote against component and level.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Arabic B lessons for Dubai families run one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. For this subject the format is a mild advantage rather than a concession, because shared audio with precise replay is what listening practice needs and because the oral rehearsal recording is kept for the student to mark themselves.

process.title: Send a marked mock, not a description
process.description: The most recent Arabic B paper with marks on it, ideally with the criterion breakdown. If the school marked a full mock, that single document usually identifies which of the three components is producing the grade, which is the question the first session exists to answer.

process.title: Free trial spent diagnosing the component
process.description: The trial session re-marks the writing against language, message and conceptual understanding, runs five minutes of listening at exam speed, and asks the student to speak for two minutes on an unseen image. Three numbers out, and a priority order. No card is required for the trial.

process.title: Write down the component order
process.description: Paper 2 first if listening is the hole, text type first if criterion C is the hole, oral first if the school window is close. The order and the reason go in writing with dates, so at week eight it is possible to check whether the plan was right rather than argue about it.

process.title: Weekly session on a three-component rotation
process.description: Sessions run live online in Gulf Standard Time, generally after 18:00 on a Dubai weekday. The rotation keeps all three components live, with one marked written piece every fortnight and the student's error list updated from their own work each round.

whyPoints.title: The three components treated separately
whyPoints.description: Arabic B grades hide which component is failing. We diagnose writing, Paper 2 and the oral independently, and build the plan from whichever is lowest rather than from the course order. A student weak only in listening should not spend a term polishing essays.

whyPoints.title: Text type conventions taught as a finite list
whyPoints.description: Six conceptual understanding marks are available for about a fortnight of attention to how each text type opens, addresses its reader and signs off. It is the highest return per hour on the whole paper and it is the work most often skipped.

whyPoints.title: Listening drilled the way it actually improves
whyPoints.description: Short audio spans, transcription and replay rather than whole papers. Shared clean audio with precise replay control is one of the few concrete advantages of a live online lesson over a tutor sitting at the kitchen table with a phone.

whyPoints.title: Error lists built from the student's own scripts
whyPoints.description: A fluent heritage speaker does not need a grammar course; they need their twelve to twenty recurring substitutions written down and checked before submission. Items leave the list when they stop appearing, which makes progress countable.

whyPoints.title: A straight answer on Arabic B versus Arabic A
whyPoints.description: Where a reading diagnostic suggests your child is in the wrong course, we say so, even when the honest answer costs us the booking. The subject decision belongs to your child's DP coordinator; the diagnostic just makes it evidence-based.

whyPoints.title: Scope stated before you buy a term
whyPoints.description: Text type, structure and accuracy respond inside six weeks. Vocabulary breadth and fluent listening do not, because both need exposure hours. Saying which is which in advance is how a family decides how much tutoring is worth buying.

faqs.question: How much does an Arabic B tutor cost per hour in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published rate cards and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table put qualified online subject tutors in Dubai at roughly AED 150-300 an hour, IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200-450, budget or university-student tutors at AED 45-150, and in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180-500 with travel sitting inside the billed hour. Those are market figures from October 2026, not IB Gram's prices. We begin with a free trial lesson and quote against level and component, because an oral intensive before a school recording window and a weekly Paper 2 rebuild are different pieces of work.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Arabic B SL and Arabic B HL?
faqs.answer: Higher Level studies two literary works and Standard Level studies none, which is the structural difference that matters most. HL also has a longer Paper 1, an hour and a half against an hour and a quarter, and a longer listening component, an hour against forty-five minutes. The weightings are the same at both levels: Paper 1 25%, Paper 2 50%, individual oral 25%. The oral itself differs, starting from a visual stimulus at SL and from a literary extract at HL, so HL preparation has to begin while the works are being taught.

faqs.question: Why does my child score well on Arabic B writing but badly overall?
faqs.answer: Because Paper 1 writing is only 25% of the grade and Paper 2 is 50%. Listening and reading together outweigh the component most students practise, and listening is the one almost nobody drills alone because doing so is unrewarding. A student with solid written Arabic and a weak Paper 2 will land a grade that looks inexplicable next to their classwork. The marked mock usually shows it immediately. The remedy is a listening and reading block worked by question type, not more essays, however much better essays feel to produce.

faqs.question: What are the five prescribed themes in Arabic B?
faqs.answer: Identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. They are contexts rather than vocabulary lists, which is the misreading that costs marks. Paper 1 tasks are set within them and the individual oral moves through them, so useful preparation means arriving with two or three positions you could defend in each, not forty memorised nouns. Dubai students have an underused advantage here: every theme has a specific local example to hand, from residency and identity to desalination under sharing the planet, and specifics read as real content in the oral.

faqs.question: How is the Arabic B individual oral marked at Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Out of 30, across language, message and interactive skills, over fifteen minutes with preparation time beforehand. The student presents a visual stimulus linked to one of the five themes, holds a conversation about it, then discusses at least one further theme. Marks are lost most often by describing the image rather than arguing from it, because a description leaves nothing for the message criterion and gives the conversation no foundation. Cold practice on unseen images, with the recording played back and self-marked, moves this faster than any amount of rereading theme notes.

faqs.question: My child is in Arabic B but speaks Arabic at home. Are they in the right course?
faqs.answer: Possibly not. Heritage speakers are routinely placed in Arabic B because their written Arabic looks weak, when the real limit is fusha reading speed rather than language ability. The test is whether they can read an unfamiliar Modern Standard Arabic page at reasonable pace and discuss it. If they can, Arabic A: Literature is within reach and dialect interference in their writing is correctable. If they decode slowly and lose the thread, Arabic B is genuinely the better fit. Raise it in DP1 with the DP coordinator, while the timetable can still change.

faqs.question: What text types can come up on Arabic B Paper 1?
faqs.answer: A blog post, a formal email or letter, an article, a speech, a report, a review, a diary entry, a set of instructions, a proposal or an interview, among others. The task names the type, and six of the thirty marks go to getting audience, purpose, context and register right for it. A strong essay written where a speech was requested keeps the language marks and forfeits those six entirely. Each type has a short list of conventions, which makes this a fortnight of learning rather than a term, and the highest return per hour on the paper.

faqs.question: How do we practise Arabic B listening when there is nothing to practise with?
faqs.answer: Use any clean Modern Standard Arabic audio and change the method rather than hunting for exam material. Take three to five minutes of recording. Play ten seconds, transcribe what was heard including the gaps, replay, fill in, replay once more, then read the transcript. The aim at this stage is not comprehension but training the ear to segment connected fusha speech, which is the actual bottleneck for students who hear dialect daily and fusha only in lessons. Twenty minutes three times a week outperforms one full paper at the weekend.

faqs.question: Do the two HL literary works appear on the Arabic B written papers?
faqs.answer: No. The two works studied at Higher Level exist mainly to supply the extract the HL individual oral starts from, and they are not examined on Paper 1 or Paper 2. That is precisely why students neglect them: they look optional relative to the written papers. A student who skimmed both arrives at the oral with no foothold when an extract is placed in front of them. Annotating both texts for themes, characters and a few quotable moments during DP1, then practising cold on extracts, is what makes the HL oral manageable.

faqs.question: Can an Arabic B tutor come to our villa in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE, and home visits are a service we run only in India. Arabic B tuition for Dubai families is delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, which usually means an evening slot on a weekday or a weekend morning. For this subject the online format is mildly better rather than worse: listening work needs clean shared audio with precise replay control, and oral rehearsals can be recorded for the student to mark themselves before the tutor comments.

faqs.question: Which grammar mistakes cost Arabic B candidates the most marks?
faqs.answer: The same families recur on almost every script we see: hamza placement, feminine endings written as haa instead of taa marbuta, alif maqsura confusion, broken plurals avoided by using singulars, idafa constructions built in the wrong order, and the reverse agreement of numbers three to ten applied the ordinary way round. The language criterion is twelve of the thirty marks on Paper 1 and twelve on the oral, so these are expensive. The method that works is a numbered personal error list drawn from the student's own marked work, checked before every submission.

faqs.question: Is six weeks of Arabic B tutoring before the exams worth it?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on which problem you have. Six weeks will reliably fix text type conventions, Paper 1 structure, reading question technique, visual stimulus handling and a named set of recurring accuracy errors. Six weeks will not build broad vocabulary or fluent listening from a low base, because both are functions of exposure hours that cannot be compressed. So the honest answer is yes if the marks are being lost on technique, and only partly if the gap is exposure. The trial session tells you which, before you commit to a block.

faqs.question: How does mandatory school Arabic relate to the Arabic B Diploma course?
faqs.answer: They are separate obligations. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools whatever international curriculum the school is licensed for, and KHDA sets requirements for how they are taught, including separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language. Arabic B is a Diploma Group 2 subject your child has chosen and is examined on by the IB. The mandatory provision is not satisfied or replaced by tutoring, and it is sometimes a different teacher with a different report, which is worth clarifying before chasing feedback.

faqs.question: Does a private Arabic tutor in the UAE need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is applied for through MoHRE's smart app, website and e-services system. Those offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Eligibility is broad, covering registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Being eligible and holding the permit are different things, so ask the tutor directly. IB Gram holds no regulator licence and claims none.

faqs.question: What should we expect to see after two months of Arabic B sessions?
faqs.answer: Four marked written pieces with language, message and conceptual understanding scored separately, a listening record kept as marks per question type rather than as a total, and at least two recorded oral attempts the student has marked themselves. Criterion C should be the first thing to move, because text type conventions are learnable quickly. Language marks move more slowly and should show the error list shortening. If nothing has moved in eight weeks, the diagnosis was wrong, the student is not working between sessions, or the match is poor, and we will say which we think it is.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.closingHeading: Start by finding out which component is actually failing
dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-home-tutor.closingBody: An Arabic B grade tells you something is wrong. It does not tell you whether the problem is writing, listening, reading or the oral, and those four need different work. Send the most recent marked mock and the date of the school's oral window, and the free trial lesson produces three component scores and a priority order you keep whichever way you decide. Sessions run one-to-one online in Gulf Standard Time. If the diagnostic says your child belongs in Arabic A rather than Arabic B, we will tell you that too.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-online-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Diploma Arabic B at Standard and Higher Level. Each one works in Modern Standard Arabic as the language of instruction, uses the five prescribed themes as the planning spine, and marks written work against the published criteria before the lesson that discusses it.

intro.heading: Arabic B is a written-language subject wearing a spoken-language label
paragraphs: Most Dubai families who search for an IB DP Arabic B online tutor are not looking for conversation practice. They are looking for a fix to a specific and very common mismatch. The child speaks Arabic fluently at home, follows a family conversation without effort, and then sits a Diploma Paper 1 task and loses marks on orthography, agreement and register. Arabic B assesses Modern Standard Arabic in writing, under timed conditions, against three named criteria. Fluency at the dinner table does not transfer to that paper automatically, and nobody at school has the timetable space to say so.

The subject sits inside Group 2 of the Diploma, the language acquisition group, at Standard or Higher Level. Both levels share the same five prescribed themes: identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. Both are assessed through Paper 1, which is a single piece of writing worth a quarter of the grade; Paper 2, which is listening and reading and carries half; and the individual oral, which is internally assessed and carries the remaining quarter. Higher Level adds two literary works studied in Arabic, and the Higher Level oral is built on an extract from one of them rather than on a photograph.

That structure decides what a useful lesson looks like. A session that only talks has covered a quarter of the assessment. A session that only drills grammar has covered none of it directly, because no criterion awards marks for grammar in isolation: Criterion A rewards the range and accuracy of language in service of the task, Criterion B rewards the message against what the task asked for, and Criterion C rewards conceptual understanding, which in practice means text type, register and audience. Students who write well and score badly are almost always losing Criterion B and C marks on a task they answered beside rather than answered.

Dubai adds a second layer that no other market has. KHDA requires Arabic in every private school in the emirate regardless of the licensed curriculum, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, so most Diploma students carrying Arabic B are also carrying a school Arabic requirement that is assessed differently, taught from Ministry-set content, and reported separately. Parents reasonably assume the two are the same subject. They are not, and tuition that treats them as one wastes half the hour.

What one-to-one online tuition changes here is the size of the pool. Diploma Arabic B is a narrow specialism: a tutor needs Modern Standard Arabic at academic register, familiarity with the current subject guide, and the patience to mark text types rather than correct sentences. Across a single Dubai community, the number of people who meet that description and are free at 5pm on a Tuesday is very small. Delivering the lesson over live video removes the twenty-minute radius from the decision, which is the whole reason this page exists.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Arabic appears in all three IB programmes a Dubai school may be authorised for, and it behaves differently in each. The notes below describe how the subject is organised at each stage and what that means for a student heading towards Arabic B in the Diploma years.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic B sits in Group 2 as a language acquisition course at Standard or Higher Level. Assessment is Paper 1 writing at 25 per cent, Paper 2 listening and reading at 50 per cent, and the internally assessed individual oral at 25 per cent. Higher Level adds two literary works and bases the oral on an extract from one of them. The five prescribed themes frame every task, and conceptual understanding of text type is marked explicitly.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the Diploma is the smaller of the two post-16 routes by enrolment, with International Baccalaureate schools accounting for 7 per cent of private-school enrolment against 37 per cent for the UK curriculum, on KHDA's 2024-25 figures. That makes Diploma Arabic B a small cohort inside a small cohort, and it is why a student is often the only person in their year group taking Arabic B at Higher Level.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic is taught as language acquisition in phases rather than year groups, so two students in the same class may sit in different phases. Assessment uses four criteria covering comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating in response to text, and using language in spoken and written form. The phase a student finishes MYP in largely decides whether Arabic B at Higher Level is realistic.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's MYP cohort is unusual because a large share of students arrive mid-programme from another system, often with Arabic study that stopped and restarted. A student entering Year 10 from a British school in another emirate may have three years of mandatory Arabic and no phase record at all, and the school places them on evidence collected in the first fortnight.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Arabic appears as an additional language inside transdisciplinary units rather than as a discrete subject with papers. There is no external assessment, so the useful signal for parents is whether the child can decode unfamiliar words and write a connected sentence by the end of Year 6. Those two skills, not vocabulary breadth, are what decide how much ground has to be made up later.
programmes.countryNote: KHDA sets mandatory Arabic from the start of primary in Dubai private schools, and its guidance on instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with the advice that any mandatory-subject lesson runs for at least 25 minutes. Schools may restructure the timetable provided weekly totals are met, which is why two Dubai schools can both comply and still deliver very different amounts of reading practice.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: A Diploma student rarely needs Arabic B alone. The list below covers the subjects Dubai families most often pair with it, with a note on what each one is actually assessed on, so a combined plan can be built around the heaviest deadline rather than the loudest complaint.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: The page's subject. Marks are lost on Criterion C more than anywhere else: a student writes a competent piece of prose where the task asked for a blog post, a formal letter or a set of instructions, and the text-type conventions were never taught as content.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Group 1 route for students who use Arabic as a school language. It assesses literary and non-literary analysis in Arabic, not language acquisition. Students sometimes sit in Arabic B when Arabic A would suit them better, and the misplacement shows up as boredom rather than as low marks.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: Designed for genuine beginners and restricted to students with little or no previous exposure to the language. Its prescribed topics are narrower and its written tasks much shorter than Arabic B's. A student who has had years of school Arabic in Dubai is generally not eligible, however weak their marks look.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The commonest Group 1 pairing in Dubai. Paper 1 is unseen guided analysis, and students who find Arabic B's Criterion C hard usually find the same conceptual work hard here. Teaching text type once, across both subjects, is more efficient than teaching it twice.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Sits at the opposite end of the week from a language subject and competes for the same revision hours. The practical reason it matters on this page is the internal assessment: the mathematics exploration deadline usually lands in the same term as the Arabic B oral.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Popular in Dubai and useful to Arabic B students because its command terms overlap. A student who can distinguish describe, explain and evaluate in Business can be shown the same distinction inside an Arabic B writing task without learning a new vocabulary of instruction.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Assessed heavily through extended writing and source work. For an Arabic B student the transferable skill is paragraph shape: a claim, support, and a link back to the question. The same structure earns Criterion B marks in Arabic, where students often supply content with no visible argument.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram-led and definition-heavy, with internal assessment commentaries drawn from news articles. The commentary habit of reading a text for its argument rather than its vocabulary is directly useful in the Arabic B reading paper, where questions reward inference over recognition.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The exhibition and the essay both ask students to handle abstraction in writing. Students who struggle to hold a position in English often cannot hold one in Arabic either, and the Arabic B conceptual criterion is where that weakness becomes a mark penalty.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Can be written in Arabic as a Group 2 essay, which is a serious undertaking and a genuine differentiator on a university application. A tutor's role here is teaching research method and giving feedback on the student's own drafts, never supplying text.

dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-online-tutor.regionsTitle: Where Dubai's Arabic B students are, and what that does to a session time
dubai/ib-dp-arabic-b-online-tutor.regionsIntro: Arabic B students are spread thinly across the emirate rather than concentrated in one or two communities, which is exactly why a local search returns so little. The notes below describe what each area does to the practical question of when a lesson can start.

regions.name: Jumeirah
regions.note: A dense cluster of IB and British schools within a short radius, so pick-up finishes early and a 4.30pm start is realistic. Many families here run two or three subject tutors in parallel, which makes a fixed weekly slot more valuable than a flexible one.

regions.name: Al Barsha
regions.note: Several large IB and British schools sit close together, and Al Barsha households often include a child in MYP Arabic and a sibling in Diploma Arabic B. Sequential online slots on the same evening work well because no travel sits between them.

regions.name: Mirdif

sections.heading: What a search for an Arabic B tutor in Dubai is usually about
paragraphs: Three distinct problems bring Dubai parents to this search, and they need different lessons. The first is a fluent speaker scoring in the middle band: the child talks easily, understands everything, and writes Arabic that reads like transcribed speech. Marks are lost on register, on orthography and on text type. The second is a student placed in Arabic B who has had years of patchy school Arabic and cannot follow the Paper 2 audio at Diploma speed. The third is a Higher Level student who is comfortable in the language but has never read a literary work in Arabic and now has an oral built on an extract from one.

These three cases look identical on a report card, which usually shows a 4 or a 5 and a comment about effort. They are not identical. The fluent speaker needs editing discipline and text-type conventions and could gain a grade in a term. The patchy-exposure student needs listening volume and a vocabulary base, which takes longer and should start a year before the exam. The Higher Level literature case needs reading support on two specific texts, which no generic Arabic tutor can give without reading them first.

The diagnostic that separates them takes about twenty minutes and is the first thing a trial lesson should do. Give the student an unseen Paper 1 task, let them write under time, and read what comes back. Orthography errors with sound argument point one way. Correct spelling with no argument points another. An inability to start at all usually means the task's text type was never understood, which is a Criterion C problem masquerading as a confidence problem. Everything on the rest of this page assumes that diagnosis has happened first, because planning a two-year language subject on a report-card grade alone is guesswork.
bullets: Fluent speaker, mid-band marks: register, orthography and text type
Patchy school Arabic: listening volume and core vocabulary, started early
Higher Level literature gap: reading support on the school's two chosen works
A twenty-minute unseen writing task tells you which case you have

sections.heading: Arabic A, Arabic B or Arabic ab initio: how the route gets decided
paragraphs: Three Arabic routes run through the Diploma and students are routinely in the wrong one. The school makes the placement, usually in the spring of Year 11, on evidence from MYP phase records, an internal assessment, and what the parent says at home. Each of those three inputs is unreliable on its own. Phase records transfer badly between schools. Internal assessments are often short. And parents reasonably describe a child who chats with grandparents as fluent, when what the Diploma assesses is the formal written register that nobody chats in.

The most consequential error runs in one direction. A strong home speaker placed in Arabic B rather than Arabic A will typically coast to a 6 and resent the course, which costs them nothing in points but wastes two years of Group 2 study. The reverse error, a student with modest Arabic placed in Arabic A, is far more damaging and much harder to unwind after the first term. The third error is a Dubai speciality: a student with years of mandatory school Arabic asking to switch to ab initio because the marks are low. Ab initio is restricted to students with little or no prior exposure, and a Dubai school Arabic record generally rules it out.

The table below sets out what each route is designed for. Take it to the Diploma coordinator rather than to the Arabic department, because the decision is a timetable and eligibility decision as much as a language one. Ask specifically what evidence was used, whether the student's MYP phase was recorded at the previous school, and what the deadline for changing is. In most Dubai schools that deadline sits early in Year 12, and after it a change means dropping and restarting a two-year course.

sections.heading: How Arabic B is assessed, component by component
paragraphs: The assessment model is the same across Group 2 languages, so anything written here about Arabic B holds for French B or Spanish B too. Paper 1 is a single piece of writing produced from a choice of three tasks, each tied to one of the prescribed themes, and each specifying a text type. Standard Level candidates write 250 to 400 words; Higher Level candidates write 450 to 600. It carries a quarter of the final grade and it is marked on three criteria: Criterion A for language, Criterion B for message, and Criterion C for conceptual understanding, which is where text type, register and audience are judged.

Paper 2 carries half the grade and is sat as one paper in two halves. The listening section comes first and the reading section follows, with the Higher Level listening section running longer than the Standard Level one. Recordings are played twice and candidates cannot control them, which makes note-taking technique a scoring skill rather than a study habit. The reading section uses authentic texts at a range of registers and asks inference and reference questions that reward reading the whole text before answering.

The individual oral is internally assessed by the school and externally moderated, and it carries the last quarter. At Standard Level the student is given a visual stimulus linked to one of the themes, prepares under supervision, presents, and then answers follow-up questions before moving to a wider conversation on other themes. At Higher Level the stimulus is an extract from one of the two literary works studied on the course. Four criteria apply, covering language, the message in response to the stimulus, the message in conversation, and interactive skills. Language and interactive skills together carry twice the weight of the two message criteria, which is why a student who answers accurately but minimally scores lower than one who talks fluently with a few errors.

sections.heading: Where Arabic B marks are actually lost
paragraphs: Orthography does the most damage and gets the least teaching. Hamza placement, the difference between ta marbuta and a final ha, alif maqsura against a final ya, and the sun and moon letter rules in writing all produce errors that a fluent speaker never hears because speech does not distinguish them. Each one is a small Criterion A deduction, and across a 500-word Higher Level task they accumulate into a band. The fix is mechanical rather than conceptual: an error log kept across a term, with the same categories revisited until they stop appearing.

Register is the second loss, and it is a conceptual one. Modern Standard Arabic has a formal written range that dialect does not provide, and students substitute a colloquial construction that is perfectly intelligible and plainly wrong for the task. Verb-subject agreement in formal written Arabic, the use of the dual, and the broken plural patterns are the usual casualties. A student who reads Arabic news reporting for fifteen minutes a day for a term absorbs more of this than any amount of grammar instruction delivers, because register is learned by exposure and corrected by feedback.

The third loss is text type, and it is the one nobody is taught. A Paper 1 task naming a blog post expects a blog post: a title, a voice, an audience and the conventions that go with them. A task naming a set of guidelines expects imperative structures and no personal narrative. Students who write a good essay in response to every task cap themselves on Criterion C. Teaching the eight or nine text types that recur, with a model and a checklist for each, is a term's work and the single highest-return thing a tutor can do on this subject. The same is true of the oral: a candidate who answers in one sentence loses interactive marks that no vocabulary work can recover.

sections.heading: Modern Standard Arabic against the Arabic spoken at home
paragraphs: Arabic is a diglossic language, which means a formal written variety and a set of spoken varieties coexist and do different jobs. Modern Standard Arabic is what newspapers, broadcast news, textbooks and the Diploma use. Emirati, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi dialects are what families use. A child raised in Dubai may hear three or four dialects in a week and no Modern Standard Arabic outside a classroom. That is the structural reason a fluent speaker can struggle in Arabic B, and it is almost never explained to parents in those terms.

The practical consequences are specific. Negation differs between varieties, so a student writes a dialect negation in a formal task. Question formation differs. Future marking differs. Numbers behave differently, and the agreement rules for numbers in formal written Arabic catch out speakers who have never needed them. Vocabulary diverges most of all: everyday nouns that differ between dialect and the standard variety are exactly the words a student reaches for under exam pressure. None of this is a deficiency in the child's Arabic. It is a different variety doing a different job.

A session that takes diglossia seriously is a different session. It treats the student's dialect as an asset for the oral's interactive criterion, where confidence and flow are rewarded, while building the standard variety deliberately for the papers. It uses reading aloud of standard text to train the ear towards Paper 2 audio, which is delivered in Modern Standard Arabic and is the component home fluency helps least with. And it stops apologising for the mismatch, because a student who understands why they are losing marks stops concluding that they are bad at their own language.

sections.heading: KHDA's mandatory Arabic and how it sits beside Diploma Arabic B
paragraphs: KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the international curriculum a school is licensed to teach, with the requirements to be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, and from April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. The authority also requires schools to organise separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, combined classes for Arab and non-Arab students are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ.

Language of instruction is specified rather than left open. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language, and as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, while non-Arab students receive Islamic Education and the moral, social and cultural strand in their school's licensed-curriculum language. Schools must also ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided weekly totals are met, and the guidance advises at least 25 minutes for any mandatory-subject lesson.

One rule matters directly for tuition. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. A tutor supporting a child's school Arabic therefore works on the skills the Ministry-set content demands rather than substituting a parallel syllabus, and a tutor supporting Diploma Arabic B works from the IB subject guide instead. Those are two jobs, two sets of criteria and often two different reports home. Families who understand the split stop asking why the school Arabic grade and the Diploma Arabic B grade move in opposite directions.

sections.heading: What Arabic tuition costs in Dubai, and what online changes
paragraphs: Dubai's tutoring market publishes very little in dirhams, which makes the figures below unusual rather than authoritative. They are market rates collected from providers' own published pages and from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 rate table, with each band attributed to whoever published it. They are not IB Gram's price list. What they do show clearly is that format, not subject, drives the number: the same tutor delivering the same hour costs materially more when a car is involved, because travel time is working time and somebody pays for it.

Arabic B sits at the specialist end of the market for a supply reason. The pool of tutors who can teach Modern Standard Arabic at academic register, know the current Diploma subject guide, and mark text types against the published criteria is small in absolute terms. Restrict that pool to people who will drive to one Dubai community at 5pm and it becomes very small indeed. Online delivery is what keeps the match possible at a sane rate, because it is drawn from a pool defined by subject rather than by postcode.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, which for a language subject is closer to parity than it is for a practical science. Writing is shared on screen and annotated live. Audio is played and replayed under exam conditions. Oral practice is recorded, played back and reviewed, which is harder to do well across a dining table. The one genuine loss is informal conversation before and after the hour, and a tutor who builds two minutes of it into the session recovers most of that.
