process.title: Send the portfolio, not a description of it
process.description: Share access to the CAS portfolio or export whatever exists, plus the DP year, the school, and whether the three interviews have happened. If the portfolio is empty, say so. An empty portfolio with fifteen months behind it is a different problem from a full one with no reflections.

process.title: Free audit session against the seven outcomes
process.description: Sixty minutes with the portfolio open. Each outcome gets marked evidenced, partly evidenced or missing, the project is checked against the duration and collaboration requirements, and the interview status is confirmed. You keep the written gap list. No card is taken to book it.

process.title: Hear the honest recommendation, including zero
process.description: In most DP1 cases the recommendation is that no paid sessions are needed and the student should take the gap list to their coordinator. We would rather say that than sell a block, because a weekly CAS slot has no work to fill it.

process.title: If needed, two or three short sessions
process.description: Reflection coaching, project sequencing or DP2 triage, booked as short sessions rather than a standing hour. The student writes every entry during or after the session; nothing is written for them, which is both the rule and the only version that survives an interview.

process.title: Take the gap list to the school
process.description: Only the school can confirm CAS completion, so every output of our work is designed to be handed over. The student goes to their coordinator with specific questions instead of a general worry, which is usually what converts a vague concern into a solved one.

process.title: Check again before each interview
process.description: A short review before the second and third documented interviews catches a missing outcome while there is still time. That is the whole of what most families need across two years: three short conversations, spaced, with the portfolio open.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you to buy nothing
whyPoints.description: Most DP1 students with a sustained activity, a creative commitment and some real service need no CAS sessions. That is the recommendation we give in the trial, and it is why this page spends more space explaining the requirement than selling against it.

whyPoints.title: Audited against the seven outcomes by name
whyPoints.description: The output of a first session is a written list showing each outcome as evidenced, partly evidenced or missing, plus the project's status against its duration and collaboration requirements. That list is specific enough to take to a coordinator.

whyPoints.title: Reflection taught as a skill, not written for the student
whyPoints.description: Four sentences: what I expected, what happened, what was hard, what I would change. We teach that shape and ask the questions that recover the detail, and the student writes every entry. A portfolio in someone else's voice fails at the interview.

whyPoints.title: Projects designed to be smaller
whyPoints.description: A six-week project that actually runs evidences far more than an ambitious one that collapses on a permission. We push towards scope the student group controls, with a fallback that needs nobody's approval, because that is what completion requires.

whyPoints.title: Built for the Dubai calendar
whyPoints.description: The long summer absence, service permission timelines, cross-city placements that break in term two, and Ramadan as either a gap or the best service month. CAS planning here fails on logistics, so the logistics are planned first.

whyPoints.title: Clear about what only the school can do
whyPoints.description: We do not confirm completion, sign anything or speak to a coordinator on your behalf. Everything we produce is designed for the student to hand over, because CAS completion is the school's decision and any provider implying otherwise has misread the component.

faqs.question: Does CAS count towards my child's IB points total?
faqs.answer: No. CAS is not assessed and contributes no points to the 45 available. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay are graded A to E and pair in a matrix worth up to three points; CAS sits outside that entirely. What CAS does instead is gate the award: a candidate who has not completed it does not receive the diploma, whatever their subject points. So it is simultaneously the component with no marks and the component with the harshest consequence, which is why the practical advice is about completion and record-keeping rather than about quality or impressiveness.

faqs.question: How many CAS hours does my daughter actually need?
faqs.answer: The current CAS guide sets no total hours figure. The expectation is engagement across at least eighteen months with a reasonable balance across creativity, activity and service, evidenced through the seven learning outcomes. The hundred and fifty hour figure still circulating in Dubai parent groups belongs to an older version of the programme. Your child's school may set its own logging requirement above the IB's, and if so that applies and should be met, so ask the coordinator directly whether a number they have given you comes from the current guide or from school policy.

faqs.question: Which CAS learning outcome do students most often miss?
faqs.answer: In Dubai it is the one about initiating and planning a CAS experience, and the reason is structural rather than personal. Schools, clubs and compounds here organise a great deal, so a student can accumulate genuinely good experiences without having started any of them. Evidencing that outcome needs a decision the student made, a plan they wrote, and usually a problem they had to deal with. The second most common gap is challenges and new skills, because a long-standing activity continued at the same level does not evidence anything new however accomplished the student is.

faqs.question: Does a one-day charity fundraiser count as the CAS project?
faqs.answer: No. The project must extend over at least a month, and students consistently read that as a month of accumulated effort rather than a month of elapsed time. A single event with a week of preparation is an experience, which is fine as an experience, but a coordinator will not accept it as the project. The other requirement it often fails is collaboration: roles that genuinely depended on each other, with decisions made jointly. A smaller project running six real weeks evidences more outcomes than a large one-day event with four names attached.

faqs.question: My son has done plenty but written nothing in his portfolio. Is that recoverable?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and it is the most common situation we see. The work exists; the evidence does not. Clearing a reflection backlog is a chronological exercise: take each experience while the memory is still there, and write four sentences on what was expected, what happened, what was difficult and what would change. Two or three sessions of reflection coaching is normally enough to teach the shape and clear the queue, and the student writes every entry. A portfolio written by anyone else fails at the final interview, which is a conversation about his own experience.

faqs.question: What are the three CAS interviews and what happens in them?
faqs.answer: They are documented conversations with a CAS coordinator or adviser, required across the programme. The first sits near the start and establishes intentions and a plan. The second sits in the middle and checks progress against the learning outcomes. The third sits at the end and confirms completion. They are not tests and there is no mark, but they are the three occasions on which a student is told what is missing while there is still time to act. A student who has had all three on schedule rarely gets a late surprise; one who has postponed them often does.

faqs.question: Can a CAS mentor write reflections for my child?
faqs.answer: No, and nobody should offer to. The portfolio is a record of the student's own experience and development, and the final interview is a conversation about it, so reflections in somebody else's voice are exposed almost immediately. What a mentor can legitimately do is explain what each outcome accepts as evidence, ask the questions that recover what was actually difficult, and teach the four-sentence shape that makes reflection quick. The student writes it. We say this before a first session rather than after an awkward request, because it is the whole basis of the work.

faqs.question: We are abroad for seven weeks every summer. Does that break CAS?
faqs.answer: Not by itself, but it is the single biggest practical risk to CAS in Dubai. The summer sits in the middle of the eighteen-month span and usually right where a project should be gathering momentum, so commitments lapse and host organisations move on. Two things prevent the damage: a project started early enough that a pause does not kill it, and a commitment that can continue in some form while away, even at reduced intensity. Experiences completed abroad count perfectly well, provided they are recorded with reflections at the time rather than reconstructed in September.

faqs.question: How does a Dubai student find a genuine service placement?
faqs.answer: Start in DP1, because permissions take weeks. Organisations working with vulnerable people reasonably take time over a sixteen-year-old volunteer, and a student who decides in DP2 that they need direct service often finds the approval timeline longer than the time left. The alternatives are legitimate rather than consolation prizes: indirect service producing something a named organisation asked for, advocacy with a real audience and measurable reach, or research work a community group actually needs. Choose one deliberately and early. Your school's CAS coordinator usually holds a list of organisations already cleared to take students.

faqs.question: Is Ramadan a good or bad month for CAS in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Both, depending on planning. School hours shorten and routines change, so standing activities pause and a student relying on a weekly pattern loses a month. At the same time there is more organised community service in this month than in any other, and students who plan for it rather than around it frequently log the strongest service experience of their programme. The condition is advance arrangement, because places fill. Mentoring sessions during the month move to post-Iftar slots, which is straightforward online and difficult for anyone driving across the city before Iftar.

faqs.question: My child transferred to a Dubai school mid-DP. Does previous CAS work still count?
faqs.answer: Generally yes. Experiences genuinely completed elsewhere count, and the issue is almost always documentation rather than legitimacy: the previous school recorded CAS on a different platform with different internal expectations, so the evidence has to be rewritten into the new school's portfolio. Do that immediately on arrival while the detail is still recoverable, rather than in DP2. The new coordinator will tell you what form they need it in, and will also confirm which interviews count as having happened, which is the detail families most often get wrong after a transfer.

faqs.question: Can a student fail the diploma because of CAS?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the sense that non-completion prevents the award. CAS is not graded, so there is no E to fall below, but the requirement is binary: either the coordinator can confirm completion or they cannot. A student with excellent subject results and an incomplete CAS record does not receive the diploma. This is unusual, because schools chase it, but it happens to students who postpone interviews, who never ran a qualifying project, or who arrive late in the programme with no transferable record. It is also entirely avoidable with three short conversations spread across two years.

faqs.question: What should CAS mentoring cost in Dubai, if we need it?
faqs.answer: At the general mid-market band rather than a specialist rate, because the work is mentoring rather than subject teaching. Published market figures as of October 2026: Unitors lists IB from AED 200 an hour and IGCSE from AED 150; budget providers advertise from AED 33-65; in-home visits run AED 180-500 with travel inside the rate. Most families who need anything need two to four hours in total across the whole programme. Anyone proposing a weekly CAS slot across DP2 is selling time, because the component does not contain enough work to fill it. Ask whether VAT is included.

faqs.question: Will CAS help my child's university application?
faqs.answer: The experiences will, the component will not. Admissions readers and scholarship panels respond to a sustained commitment, a real project and a student who can talk about both, which is exactly what completing CAS properly produces as a by-product. What carries no weight is the fact of completion itself, because every diploma holder has done it. So pursue the activities for their own sake and keep the record for the IB's sake, and do not spend money trying to make a CAS portfolio impressive. There is no scale on which one portfolio outranks another.

faqs.question: Do you send someone to our home in Dubai for CAS mentoring?

Dubai students are mentored one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For CAS that fits the work better: the useful session is twenty to forty minutes with the portfolio on a shared screen, which nobody wants to pay travel time for, and the pattern of attention is three short bursts across two years rather than a weekly visit. If you need an adult physically present, this is not the right service and we would rather say so.

intro.heading: Nothing in CAS is marked, and that is the problem
paragraphs: CAS awards no marks and no points. It cannot raise a Diploma score by a single point, and no examiner ever reads it. What it can do is prevent a Diploma from being awarded, because satisfactory completion is a requirement rather than a credit. That asymmetry is the whole reason CAS causes trouble in Dubai schools: a component that cannot improve an outcome but can block one attracts exactly as much student attention as its mark allocation suggests, which is none, until the term it becomes urgent.

The second structural feature is that the only assessable object is the portfolio. A student may have coached a junior football squad for eighteen months, run a beach clean every term, learned an instrument and organised a fundraiser, and still arrive at the sign-off conversation with nothing a coordinator can accept, because none of it was recorded, none of it was reflected on, and no outcome was consciously evidenced. Activity is not the requirement. Documented experience against the seven learning outcomes is the requirement.

So when a family searches for CAS help in Dubai, the thing they almost always need is not more activities. It is an audit: what the portfolio currently contains, which of the seven outcomes it genuinely evidences, which strand is thin, whether a CAS project exists that meets the duration and collaboration requirements, and which gaps can still be closed in the time left. That is an hour's work, and it produces a written document a student and a coordinator can both read.

This page is therefore organised around failure states rather than around the rules. The rules are available in the CAS guide your school holds, and they are revised periodically, so confirm every requirement with your DP coordinator rather than with any website including this one. What a page can usefully add is the diagnosis: the five states a portfolio actually arrives in, what each looks like from the coordinator's side of the desk, why it happened, and what a single session changes.

Everything is delivered one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, with the student's portfolio shared on screen. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in the UAE; tutors travelling to a family's address is a service we run only in India. For CAS that is almost beside the point, because the work is documentary and conversational and needs no apparatus. What matters more is that in a great many cases the honest advice after the first hour is to buy nothing further, and a mentor who says so is worth more than one who proposes a standing weekly slot for a component that takes ten minutes a fortnight to keep current. That recommendation is written down rather than offered in passing, so a family can act on it without a second conversation.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Experiential learning runs through the IB long before the Diploma, and what a student brings to CAS depends on which route they took. The programmes below set those habits, with a note on the one that causes trouble in a Dubai CAS portfolio.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: CAS runs across both Diploma years alongside Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay, and requires a balanced engagement with creativity, activity and service, evidence of the seven learning outcomes, at least one CAS project lasting a month or more, and three interviews with the CAS coordinator. It is not graded. Satisfactory completion is a condition of the Diploma, so the consequence of neglecting it is binary rather than incremental.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools set their own CAS deadlines, interview dates and portfolio platforms, and they vary considerably between schools. Ask the coordinator in the first term of DP1 for the interview schedule and the portfolio requirements in writing; the commonest Dubai failure is a student working to a deadline nobody confirmed.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Service as action and the Personal Project both train documentation and reflection, which is precisely the habit CAS depends on. Students from continuum schools usually understand that recording is part of the work. What MYP does not demand is sustained commitment across eighteen months, so the gap these students show is duration rather than documentation.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's large number of IB continuum schools means a substantial part of the Diploma cohort arrives with service-as-action experience. Those students should not assume that work counts: CAS runs from the start of the Diploma, and earlier commitments usually need to be restarted or explicitly continued with the coordinator's agreement.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: British-curriculum students arrive from a system with rich extracurricular provision and no requirement to document it. They have usually done plenty and recorded nothing, and they tend to treat CAS as a list of things attended rather than as evidence of learning. That is the single commonest portfolio problem in Dubai, and it is a writing and framing problem rather than an activity problem.
programmes.countryNote: With UK curriculum at 37 per cent of enrolment across Dubai private schools, this is the dominant route into the Diploma here. A student from this background usually needs one hour converting existing commitments into evidenced outcomes, not a plan for new ones.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
programmes.description: The other two core components are assessed and carry points, which is why they consume the attention CAS does not. The practical effect is that CAS work migrates into the weeks when the Extended Essay and internal coursework deadlines are already colliding. Planning CAS checkpoints around those weeks rather than into them is most of what good CAS planning consists of.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai schools the Extended Essay internal deadline, the heaviest coursework weeks and a CAS interview frequently land in the same half-term. A student who has kept the portfolio current through DP1 passes that fortnight without noticing; one who has not loses time that the assessed components needed.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: CAS is not a subject, and it has a specific relationship with the ones a student does study: experiences can inform a subject, but the same piece of work cannot be used twice. The notes below set out where the overlap is useful and where it becomes a problem.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Reflection in CAS and reflection in TOK are different animals and students conflate them. TOK asks how knowledge is produced; a CAS reflection asks what the student learned about themselves and others through doing something. Writing one in the register of the other is a common reason a portfolio entry fails to evidence an outcome.

subjects.name: The Extended Essay
subjects.description: An essay can grow out of an interest a CAS experience sparked, which is legitimate and often produces strong research questions. What cannot happen is the same work serving as both: the essay is assessed and the CAS experience is a requirement, and a coordinator will ask.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Studio practice looks like the creativity strand and is not automatically it, because work produced for assessment belongs to the subject. The usable version is separate creative activity: a community mural, a workshop taught to younger students, an exhibition organised rather than entered.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: A school production can satisfy creativity, and the assessed Theatre components cannot. Students in Dubai schools with strong drama programmes are the most likely to assume the whole of their involvement counts, and the cleanest solution is to log the production separately from any assessed task.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Learning an instrument over eighteen months is close to an ideal creativity commitment, because it demonstrates perseverance and developing skill naturally. Students who already play need to show progression and reflection rather than mere continuation, which is a framing change rather than more practice.

subjects.name: Sports, Exercise and Health Science
subjects.description: The activity strand is usually straightforward for students taking this subject, and it is also where double-counting is most tempting. Training for a team is activity; a practical investigation written up for the course is subject work, and the two need separate records.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Service opportunities with genuine environmental substance exist in Dubai, from mangrove and beach programmes to community sustainability projects. Students taking this subject can design service that is informed by it without using the same work for both, which is the distinction a coordinator checks.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Organising a fundraiser or running a small social enterprise can satisfy service and sometimes the CAS project, provided the beneficiary and the need are real and identified. The failure mode is a business-style event whose service element was assumed rather than established.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Students often want to volunteer with vulnerable groups, which raises safeguarding and consent questions schools handle carefully. Plan these through the coordinator early; a placement declined in month seventeen is a problem that an hour in DP1 would have avoided.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Engagement with issues of global significance is both a CAS learning outcome and this subject's territory, which makes the boundary worth fixing early. Advocacy work can evidence the outcome strongly when the student can say what they did, with whom, and what changed.

sections.heading: If nothing in CAS is marked, what is actually assessed?
paragraphs: An IB DP CAS online tutor in Dubai spends the first hour correcting an assumption, because most families arrive believing CAS is scored in some way. It is not. There is no mark, no grade and no external examiner, and the hours a student has accumulated are not themselves the requirement. What exists instead is a judgement by the CAS coordinator that the student has engaged with all three strands, evidenced the seven learning outcomes, completed a CAS project of at least a month, and held the required interviews.

That makes the portfolio the only object anyone can evaluate. Everything else — the coaching, the fundraising, the music lessons, the beach cleans — exists in the past and is invisible unless it was recorded. This is why students who have done a great deal can be in more trouble than students who have done less: the ones who did less often kept a tidy record because it was manageable, and the ones who did a great deal assumed the volume spoke for itself.

The table below separates the four things families routinely believe are assessed from what the requirement actually is. Confirm the current wording of the outcomes and the project requirements with your school's CAS coordinator, who holds the guide in force for your child's cohort; the point here is not to restate the rules but to show where the mismatch between effort and compliance usually sits.

The practical consequence is encouraging. A portfolio problem is a documentation problem, and documentation can be rebuilt from genuine experience far faster than experience can be manufactured. A student with eighteen months of real commitment and no record is three or four hours of their own writing away from a satisfactory portfolio. A student with a tidy record and no sustained commitment has a harder problem, because the only cure for duration is time.

sections.heading: The five states a CAS portfolio actually arrives in
paragraphs: Portfolios arriving for help in Dubai fall into five recognisable states, and the right response differs completely between them. Treating them all as the same problem — more activities, more entries — is why some families spend a term on CAS and still fail the sign-off conversation. The table names each state, what it looks like from the coordinator's side, why it happened and what one session changes.

The commonest by a wide margin is the attendance log: a portfolio full of entries, each recording what happened and when, and none of them evidencing an outcome. This is almost always a British-curriculum student with a rich extracurricular life and no habit of documentation, and it is the most recoverable state there is. The raw material is genuine; what is missing is the reflective layer, and a student can supply that themselves once somebody has shown them the difference with one worked example.

The hardest state is the one that looks fine. A balanced portfolio with regular entries and a project, where the project ran for three weeks rather than a month, or where the collaboration was nominal because the student did everything themselves, or where the identified need was assumed rather than established. Coordinators catch these at approval or at the final interview, and by then the duration requirement can be impossible to meet. This is the state the project design clinic exists to prevent.

One state is not a tutoring problem at all, and saying so is part of the job. A student in month seventeen with no sustained commitment in one strand needs a conversation with their coordinator, not with a mentor, because what they require is an accommodation or an extension that only the school can discuss. A provider who sells a block of hours into that situation is selling something that cannot work.

sections.heading: What one CAS session actually produces, stage by stage
paragraphs: The value of an hour on CAS varies more by timing than in any other part of the Diploma, because some of the requirements are satisfied only by elapsed time. An hour in the first term of DP1 can shape eighteen months of commitment; the same hour in the final term can only organise what already exists. The table sets that out explicitly, including what each hour cannot do, which is the column a family in month sixteen most needs.

Early hours are about design. A project design clinic tests a proposed CAS project against the requirements that actually sink one — duration, genuine collaboration, a real identified need, and whether the student can sustain the travel from their part of Dubai — and it costs a single hour at the point of choosing. Nothing later in the programme is as cheap, because a project approved and then abandoned in month four takes its four months with it.

Middle hours are about habit, and the honest recommendation there is usually to buy almost nothing. A student who writes a short entry after each experience, in the moment, needs no mentor; they need a reminder and a template, and one hour establishes both. Families who buy a weekly CAS slot through DP1 are paying for supervision of something that takes ten minutes a fortnight to do properly.

Late hours are about triage and are worth having, within limits. A recovery block can convert real experience into evidenced outcomes, identify which gaps a coordinator will not sign off without, and prepare a student to have a useful conversation at their final interview. What it cannot do is create a month of project duration in a fortnight or produce a commitment that was never made. Any provider implying otherwise in month seventeen is selling reassurance.

sections.heading: From diary to evidence: what a usable reflection contains
paragraphs: The single most common CAS entry in a Dubai portfolio reads like a diary. It names the activity, says when it happened, reports that it was enjoyable or tiring, and concludes that the student learned a lot. Everything in it is true and none of it evidences an outcome, because an outcome is a claim about the student's development that needs support, and enjoyment is not support.

A usable entry does four things, none of which requires good writing. It states what the student actually did, specifically enough that a reader could picture it. It names a difficulty, a surprise or a disagreement, because learning is visible at friction and invisible in smooth success. It says what the student did differently as a result. And it connects to the people involved: who else was there, what they contributed, what the student noticed about working with them. Those four moves cover most of the seven outcomes between them.

The friction point is the part students resist, and it is the part coordinators look for. A student who writes that the junior squad would not listen in week three, that they changed how they opened a session, and that attendance improved afterwards has evidenced perseverance, skill development and working with others in three sentences. A student who writes that coaching was rewarding has evidenced nothing, however rewarding it genuinely was.

Reconstructing entries later is legitimate provided it is honest, and it is also harder than writing them at the time, which is the whole argument for the ten-minute habit. Where a student is rebuilding months of entries, the useful method is to work from real detail they can still recall — a specific session, a specific conversation, a specific thing that went wrong — rather than from a general impression of the commitment. The mentor's role here is to ask the questions that surface that detail. Every word that goes into the portfolio is the student's own.

sections.heading: Strand balance and the project: the two structural checks
paragraphs: Two things about a CAS portfolio are structural rather than textual, which means no amount of good writing fixes them. The first is balance across creativity, activity and service. The requirement is for a reasonable, sustained engagement with all three over the programme, not an equal division, and the strand that collapses in Dubai is almost always service, because it is the one that usually requires a journey to somebody else's premises at a time that competes with coursework.

The fix for a thin service strand is to design something that survives a Dubai term rather than something that sounds impressive. Peer tutoring of younger students, coaching at a club the student already attends, a sustained online commitment with a recognised organisation, or a long-running community initiative near home all work, because the barrier to continuing them is low. A fortnightly commitment that actually happens for a year evidences far more than a weekly one abandoned in November.

The second structural check is the project. It must last at least a month, involve genuine collaboration, and address a real need the student has identified rather than assumed. Each of those is a place projects fail. A one-day fundraising event, however successful, does not meet the duration requirement by itself. A project where the student did all the work because the group was unreliable fails on collaboration. A project designed around what is easy to organise rather than around an identified need struggles on the outcomes about global or community significance.

Both checks are cheap in DP1 and expensive in DP2, which is the recurring theme of this page. An hour spent testing a project outline before it starts is worth more than four hours spent writing it up well afterwards, because the write-up cannot repair a structure that does not meet the requirement. And a coordinator who approves an outline early is a coordinator who will not raise a problem at the final interview, which is the conversation every family on this page is ultimately trying to make uneventful.

sections.heading: What Dubai actually makes easy, and what it makes hard
paragraphs: Dubai is a generous city for creativity and activity and a more complicated one for service. The private-school sector alone taught 387,441 students across 227 schools offering seventeen curricula in 2024-25, according to the Dubai Media Office, and the extracurricular infrastructure around that is substantial: clubs, academies, studios, performance venues and youth sport at a scale most cities do not have. A student who cannot find a creativity or activity commitment here has not looked.

Service is harder for practical reasons rather than cultural ones. Many organisations have safeguarding and age requirements, places are limited and allocated early in the term, and the journey to a placement competes with coursework on exactly the evenings coursework needs. That is why the service strand collapses more often than the other two, and why the sustainable options are usually the ones with the shortest travel: peer tutoring, work with younger children at a club already attended, community initiatives within walking distance, or a genuine online commitment.

The calendar imposes its own shape. Outdoor activity in the hottest months is limited, which pushes physical commitments into the cooler half of the year and makes summer a better window for creativity, planning and writing. Ramadan shifts the household and school rhythm, and CAS work moves comfortably to post-Iftar timing; sessions here adjust on request. A large share of Dubai families also travel for several weeks in the summer, which breaks any commitment requiring physical attendance and is survivable only if the student has planned for the interruption rather than discovered it.

Mandatory subjects are worth a note too, because they affect the week CAS has to fit into. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with KHDA requiring that schools organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and calculating instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit. A Diploma student's timetable in Dubai is therefore fuller than the IB subject list suggests, and a CAS plan built without that in mind tends to be the first thing to give.

sections.heading: The sign-off conversation, and the line a mentor does not cross
paragraphs: CAS ends in a conversation rather than an examination. The three interviews with the coordinator are the mechanism, and the final one is where satisfactory completion is confirmed. Preparing for it is legitimate and largely consists of being able to talk about one's own eighteen months: which commitment mattered most and why, what went wrong at some point, what the student would do differently, and which of the outcomes they feel they evidenced least well. A student who can answer those four honestly has very little to fear.

The boundary for a mentor is absolute and worth stating plainly, because it is the thing a family is entitled to check before paying anyone. A mentor may ask questions, explain what an outcome is asking for, show one worked example, test a project outline against the requirements, and audit a portfolio. A mentor may not write a reflection, supply the content of an entry, invent an experience, or attend an interview on the student's behalf. CAS is a record of what the student did and learned; a portfolio containing somebody else's words is not a record of anything.

That restraint is not just ethical caution. A fabricated or ghost-written portfolio is trivially exposed in an interview, because the coordinator asks follow-up questions and the student cannot answer them. Providers in this market do sell written coursework — one researched competitor advertises completed Internal Assessments outright — and under IB rules the consequence of submitting work that is not the student's own falls on the candidate and can reach the loss of the Diploma. For an unmarked component, the risk-to-reward ratio of that trade is absurd.

Two further points belong here. No tutoring provider should attach the name of a regulator — KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education — or of an examination board to language about approval, accreditation or authorisation unless it holds that specific permit and can show the number; IB Gram holds none and implies none. And private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen, applied for through MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service with no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so any figure quoted to you is unverified. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules additionally bar school staff from paid tutoring of students at their own school.

sections.heading: What CAS mentoring costs in Dubai, and when the answer is to buy none
paragraphs: Published rates for tutoring in Dubai are wide and worth knowing even for a component like this one. Budget online platforms advertise from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with EdFlik from AED 45 to AED 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52. Qualified online subject tutors sit around AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200. IB specialists run from about AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table showing AED 200 to AED 450 or more. In-home visits run roughly AED 180 to AED 500 with travel inside the rate, and premium named tutoring reaches AED 650, as BartyED publishes. Those are other providers' figures read in October 2026, not our price list.

CAS is the component where the honest advice is most often to buy nothing, and that needs saying on a page whose purpose is partly commercial. A student who is logging experiences as they happen, has a balanced set of commitments, and has a project approved by their coordinator does not need a mentor at any price. The requirement is not difficult; it is simply easy to neglect. One hour in the first term of DP1, establishing a habit and a template, is frequently the entire sensible purchase across two years.

Where paid hours do earn their fee, they cluster at three points: an hour to design and test the project before it starts, an hour to rebuild one reflection as a model when a coordinator has said the portfolio does not yet evidence the outcomes, and a short triage block if a deadline is close and the gaps are real. Three or four hours across two years, placed at those points, is a realistic maximum for most students and considerably less than a weekly arrangement would cost.

One piece of context Dubai families find useful. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in school fees for private schools in the emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under Dubai's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. School fees are fixed and outside a family's control; tutoring is not. Spending on an unmarked component should therefore be deliberate and small, and the money is better directed at the assessed parts of the Diploma. IB Gram arranges no home visits in the UAE: CAS mentoring for Dubai families is one-to-one over live video, and the first hour, including the portfolio audit, is free with no card required.

process.title: Share the portfolio and the interview dates
process.description: Send access to the portfolio as it stands, however thin, along with the school's CAS interview schedule and any written comment the coordinator has given. Those three things decide what is still possible, and the interview dates are the deadlines that actually bind rather than any IB date.

process.title: Take the free portfolio audit
process.description: One hour, online and one-to-one, no card required. The portfolio is read against the three strands and the seven learning outcomes, and a written statement comes back: what is evidenced, what is claimed but unevidenced, which strand is thin, and whether a qualifying project exists.

process.title: Decide whether anything needs buying
process.description: For a substantial share of students the audit concludes that the portfolio is adequate and the student should keep logging. That is the finding in writing, and nothing further is booked. CAS is the Diploma component where the correct recommendation is most often no paid support at all.

process.title: Fix structure before text
process.description: Where there is a real gap, the project and the strand balance are addressed first, because no amount of good writing repairs a project that does not meet the duration or collaboration requirement. Text comes second, and the student writes every word of it themselves.

process.title: Prepare for the conversation, not for a mark
process.description: The programme ends in an interview with the coordinator rather than an examination. Preparation means being able to say what mattered, what went wrong, what changed and which outcome is weakest. Rehearsing honest answers is legitimate; supplying them is not, and it fails immediately under follow-up questions.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you to buy nothing
whyPoints.description: For many students the portfolio audit ends with a recommendation to keep logging and book no further hours. CAS is unmarked and not difficult, and a provider proposing a weekly slot for it is selling supervision of something that takes ten minutes a fortnight to do properly.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis by portfolio state
whyPoints.description: An attendance log, an empty shell, an unbalanced portfolio, a project that does not qualify and a late absence of commitment are five different problems with five different fixes. Treating them as one, by adding activities, is why some families spend a term on CAS and still fail the sign-off.

whyPoints.title: Structure before writing
whyPoints.description: Duration, collaboration and an identified need are structural requirements that good prose cannot repair. We test a project outline in one hour before it starts, which is worth more than four hours spent writing up a project that did not meet the requirement in the first place.

whyPoints.title: Every word is the student's own
whyPoints.description: A mentor asks questions, explains an outcome, shows one worked example and audits a portfolio. Nobody writes a reflection for a student. A ghost-written portfolio collapses under follow-up questions in the interview, and under IB rules the consequence falls on the candidate.

whyPoints.title: Designed around the student's part of Dubai
whyPoints.description: A service commitment that requires a thirty-minute drive on a coursework evening will be abandoned by November. Plans here are built around what is actually reachable from the family's area and what survives the hot months, Ramadan and several weeks of summer travel.

whyPoints.title: An honest line on what the school must handle
whyPoints.description: Some situations are not tutoring problems. A student late in DP2 with no sustained commitment in a strand needs a conversation with their coordinator about accommodations, not a block of paid hours, and we say so rather than selling into it.

faqs.question: If CAS is not marked, what can actually go wrong?
faqs.answer: The Diploma itself. CAS awards no marks and no points, so it cannot raise a score, but satisfactory completion is a condition of the award rather than a credit towards it. That asymmetry is the whole risk: a component that cannot help but can block attracts no student attention until it becomes urgent. In practice what goes wrong is documentation rather than effort. Confirm your school's own deadlines and interview dates with the CAS coordinator, because those are the dates that bind and they differ between Dubai schools.

faqs.question: What does the CAS coordinator actually sign off?
faqs.answer: Their judgement that the student has engaged in a sustained and balanced way with creativity, activity and service, has evidenced the seven learning outcomes, has completed a CAS project meeting the duration and collaboration requirements, and has held the required interviews. It is a professional judgement about a portfolio, not the marking of a submission, which is why a conversation rather than a grade concludes it. Ask the coordinator early what their school expects to see in the portfolio; platforms and expectations vary and the answer is free.

faqs.question: Our son's portfolio is a list of activities. What is missing?
faqs.answer: The reflective layer, and it is the most recoverable problem in CAS. An entry that records what happened and when evidences attendance; an entry that names a difficulty, says what the student did differently as a result, and describes who else was involved and what they contributed evidences several outcomes at once. The raw material is already genuine. One hour rebuilding a single entry as a worked example is usually enough for a student to rewrite the rest themselves, which is exactly how it should go.

faqs.question: Can one session fix a portfolio with eighteen months of gaps?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on whether the gaps are in the record or in the commitment. If the student genuinely did things and wrote nothing, one audit hour plus several hours of their own honest writing can produce a satisfactory portfolio, because the experience exists and can be documented from real detail. If the commitment itself was never sustained, no session creates elapsed time, and the right step is a conversation with the coordinator about what the school can accommodate. An honest first hour tells you which situation you are in.

faqs.question: How do we tell whether a reflection is good enough?
faqs.answer: Read it and ask whether a stranger could tell what the student learned, and how they know. A usable entry states specifically what was done, names a friction point — a difficulty, a surprise, a disagreement — says what changed as a result, and describes the people involved and their contribution. An entry reporting that something was rewarding or that the student learned a lot fails that test, however true it is. Friction is where learning becomes visible, and smooth success evidences nothing.

faqs.question: Which CAS strand do Dubai students most often come up short in?
faqs.answer: Service, and for practical reasons rather than reluctance. Creativity and activity are abundantly available in this city through clubs, academies and studios, usually close to home or arranged through the school. Service tends to require a journey to somebody else's premises at a time that competes directly with coursework, and organisations often have safeguarding requirements and limited places allocated early in the term. The strand that survives is the one with the shortest travel, which is why peer tutoring and club-based coaching work better here than ambitious placements.

faqs.question: Is a fundraising event enough to satisfy the service strand?
faqs.answer: Rarely on its own. A single event can evidence some outcomes — planning, collaboration, perhaps initiative — but it is difficult to show sustained commitment or genuine engagement with a need from one afternoon. It also does not meet the CAS project duration requirement by itself. Fundraising works well as part of a longer commitment where the student can say who benefits and how they established that, rather than as a self-contained achievement. Check any plan with the coordinator before it runs rather than afterwards.

faqs.question: Can experiences from before the Diploma started be counted?
faqs.answer: Generally not, because CAS runs across the Diploma's two years and the programme is about engagement during that period. A commitment begun earlier can usually continue into CAS and be documented from the point the Diploma starts, which is different from importing two previous years of it. This matters particularly for students from IB continuum schools who did service as action in the MYP. Ask the coordinator how they treat continuing commitments; it is a question with a clear answer and it is worth asking in DP1.

faqs.question: The CAS deadline is close and almost nothing is written. What do we do first?
faqs.answer: Speak to the coordinator today, before buying any help. They have seen this before, they know what their school requires for sign-off, and only they can discuss any accommodation. Then triage: list the experiences that genuinely happened, identify which outcomes each can evidence, and write entries from real detail rather than general impressions. Work on the gaps the coordinator will not sign off without, in that order. An honest statement of what cannot be recovered is more useful at this point than an optimistic plan.

faqs.question: Does the CAS project have to be separate from everything else?
faqs.answer: It has to be its own thing, and it cannot double as assessed work for a subject. A project can grow from an existing commitment, but it needs genuine collaboration, a duration of at least a month, and a need the student identified rather than assumed, and it must be documented as a project with a process rather than an outcome. Work produced for a subject's assessment belongs to that subject. Coordinators ask about this specifically at approval, which is the best moment to get the boundary right.

faqs.question: How does the Dubai summer affect CAS planning?
faqs.answer: It reshapes the year rather than shortening it. Outdoor physical commitments are constrained in the hottest months, which pushes activity into the cooler half of the year and makes summer a good window for creativity, project planning and writing up entries that have fallen behind. A large share of Dubai families also travel for several weeks, which breaks anything requiring physical attendance. A plan that assumes twelve uninterrupted months will fail; one that treats the summer as a different kind of CAS period does not.

faqs.question: Can a mentor attend the CAS interview with my child?
faqs.answer: No, and no legitimate mentor would offer to. The interviews are a conversation between the student and their CAS coordinator about the student's own experience, and a third party has no place in them. What is entirely proper is preparation: being able to say which commitment mattered most and why, what went wrong at some point, what would be done differently, and which outcome feels least well evidenced. A student who can answer those honestly needs nothing else, and a student who cannot would be exposed by the first follow-up question anyway.

faqs.question: What should a student have ready for a first CAS session?
faqs.answer: Four things. Access to the portfolio exactly as it stands, however sparse. A list of what they have actually been doing for the last year, including commitments they never thought to log. Any written comment the coordinator has given. And the school's interview schedule. With those, the hour goes entirely on the audit and a written statement of position comes back the same day, rather than being spent working out what the student has been doing.

faqs.question: Is CAS mentoring something most Dubai families should buy at all?
faqs.answer: Honestly, no. A student who logs experiences as they happen, keeps a reasonable balance across the three strands and has a project approved by their coordinator needs no paid support for an unmarked component. Where hours earn their place it is at three narrow points: testing a project before it starts, rebuilding one reflection as a model when a coordinator says the outcomes are not evidenced, and a short triage block if a deadline is close and the gaps are real. Three or four hours across two years is a realistic maximum.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram arrange a CAS mentor who meets my child somewhere in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. We arrange no in-person tutoring anywhere in the UAE; mentors or tutors travelling to a family's address is a service we offer only in India. CAS mentoring for Dubai families runs one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, with the portfolio shared on screen. For this component the format costs nothing, because the work is documentary and conversational and needs no apparatus or materials. Sessions also move to post-Iftar timing during Ramadan and continue while a family is travelling over the summer.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-online-tutor.closingHeading: Audit the portfolio, then decide if you need anything
dubai/ib-dp-cas-online-tutor.closingBody: If CAS has become the thing nobody in your household can account for, start with an hour that costs nothing. Share the portfolio as it stands and the school's interview dates, and the free audit comes back as a written statement: which of the seven outcomes are genuinely evidenced, which strand is thin, whether the project meets the duration and collaboration requirements, and what each remaining gap needs. For a good number of families that document ends the matter, because the answer is to keep logging and book nothing. That is the most common correct recommendation in CAS.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.tutorsIntro: The mentors below have run or supervised CAS programmes rather than taught a syllabus. Their work is planning, evidence mapping and reflection quality — and knowing which gaps a Dubai school's coordinator will question at the final interview.

intro.heading: The component with no marks that can still cost a Diploma
paragraphs: Creativity, Activity, Service is the third core component of the Diploma and the only one that carries no grade. There is no mark scheme, no examiner and no band descriptor. What there is instead is a completion requirement: a student must provide evidence of having achieved all seven CAS learning outcomes, maintain a portfolio, complete a CAS project lasting at least one month, and attend three documented interviews with the school's coordinator. Fail to complete it and the Diploma is not awarded, whatever the six subject grades say.

That asymmetry is why CAS behaves differently from every other part of the programme. There is no upside — nobody gets extra points for an exceptional portfolio — and the downside is total. Students respond rationally by deprioritising it, because nothing is due tomorrow and nothing is marked. Then the final interview arrives, the coordinator asks for evidence of an outcome the student never addressed, and a component that was never difficult becomes urgent in the same term as the Extended Essay and final examinations.

The second thing families in Dubai consistently get wrong is the hours. The old requirement of a set number of hours was removed years ago, and there is no hour target to hit. What replaced it is harder to manage and better pedagogically: a reasonable balance across the three strands, over at least eighteen months, evidenced against the seven outcomes. Parents still ask us how many hours are needed, and schools still occasionally quote the old figure, which is how students end up logging time instead of building evidence.

The third is the nature of the work. CAS cannot be tutored, because there is nothing to learn. What can be mentored is planning: which outcomes are already covered by things the student does anyway, which are genuinely missing, how to design a CAS project that satisfies the collaboration and duration requirements without inventing a charity, what a reflection has to contain to be worth writing, and what the coordinator will ask at each of the three interviews. Most families need two or three sessions in total, and we say so rather than selling a weekly slot.

IB Gram matches your child with a CAS mentor who works one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time around the Dubai school day. Tuition and mentoring for UAE families is delivered online. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. A free trial lesson comes first, one per family, with no card details taken. The student does every activity and writes every reflection — nobody else can, and a portfolio that was not built by the student is an academic honesty problem rather than a shortcut.
bullets: CAS is not graded; completing it is a requirement for the award of the Diploma
Seven learning outcomes must all be evidenced, not just experienced
There is no hour requirement — a reasonable balance across three strands replaced it
The CAS project must run at least one month and involve collaboration
Three documented interviews with the coordinator, spread across the two years
A student's reflections and evidence must be their own work

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.programmesIntro: Service and self-directed activity appear throughout the IB, and how a student handled the earlier version usually predicts how CAS will go. These are the stages we work across in Dubai.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: CAS runs for a minimum of eighteen months, normally from the start of DP1 to the second half of DP2. The student records experiences and reflections in a portfolio, evidences all seven learning outcomes, carries out a CAS project of at least one month involving collaboration, and attends three documented interviews with the coordinator. There is no mark and no grade; there is a completion requirement.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools run very different CAS systems. Some use a structured online platform with monthly checkpoints; others rely on a single adviser and an end-of-term reminder. Ask which model your child's school uses and when the three interviews fall, because the answer decides whether outside mentoring is useful at all.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP includes service as action throughout the programme and culminates in the personal project, which is self-directed, supervised and recorded in a process journal. A student who kept that journal honestly already has the habit CAS depends on. A student who produced it retrospectively usually repeats the pattern with the CAS portfolio two years later.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has a large IB continuum population, so some DP1 students arrive with four years of service-as-action behind them while others, arriving from IGCSE, have never recorded a reflection. The second group needs a planning session in the first term, not a rescue in DP2.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme core includes service learning rather than CAS, alongside personal and professional skills, language development and the reflective project. Service learning follows a similar investigate-prepare-act-reflect cycle, so the planning and reflection coaching transfers almost unchanged.
programmes.countryNote: A small number of Dubai schools offer the CP. Families occasionally ask us for CAS help when the requirement on the registration is service learning, so the first thing we confirm is which programme the student is enrolled in and which document the coordinator actually wants.

programmes.name: CAS with TOK and the Extended Essay
programmes.description: Two core components carry points and one carries a veto. TOK and the Extended Essay are graded A to E and combine for up to three Diploma points; CAS is pass-or-not-complete. The practical difference is that CAS cannot be improved by extra effort in the final month, because the evidence has to have accumulated over at least eighteen months.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the CAS final interview frequently sits in the same weeks as the Extended Essay submission and subject internal assessment deadlines. Students who clear the portfolio before that fortnight have a materially easier DP2 than those who leave it inside it.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.subjectsIntro: CAS is organised in three strands and interacts with several Diploma subjects — including one rule that catches students out, because an experience cannot be counted twice.

subjects.name: Creativity
subjects.description: Arts and activities involving creative thinking, where the student is producing rather than consuming. Music lessons already taken, a school production, a design or coding build, a photography series. The usual gap is evidence: the activity happened and nothing records what the student initiated or how the work developed.

subjects.name: Activity
subjects.description: Physical exertion contributing to a healthy lifestyle. Club sport, swimming, martial arts, running, a training plan the student designed. Dubai families usually have this strand covered before DP1 starts, which makes it the cheapest place to evidence commitment and perseverance if the training is recorded as it happens.

subjects.name: Service
subjects.description: Collaborative, unpaid engagement with a community in response to an identified need, with a learning benefit for the student. This is the strand that stalls most often in Dubai, because a genuine need has to be identified rather than assumed and the organisation has to be one the school will accept.

subjects.name: The CAS project
subjects.description: A challenge of at least one month that involves collaboration and addresses one or more of the three strands, taken through investigation, preparation, action, reflection and demonstration. One month is a minimum, not a target, and a project designed in a week usually fails the collaboration requirement rather than the duration one.

subjects.name: Sports, Exercise and Health Science
subjects.description: Overlaps with the activity strand in content but not in credit: work assessed for a Diploma subject cannot also be submitted as a CAS experience. Students taking this subject often assume their practical work covers the strand, and coordinators rightly ask for something separate.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: The same double-counting rule applies. Studio work produced for the exhibition or the process portfolio belongs to the subject, not to creativity. A separate creative commitment — a community mural, a workshop run for younger students, an exhibition organised rather than entered — keeps the two clearly distinct.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Strong material for creativity provided the CAS experience is additional to assessed coursework. Running a drama club for primary students, stage-managing a production outside the course, or taking a show to a community venue all evidence initiative in a way a graded performance cannot.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Most Dubai students already have lessons, ensembles or a band, which covers creativity if recorded properly. The outcome that needs attention is usually new skills or perseverance: four years of grade examinations is commitment, and the portfolio needs to show what developed rather than that attendance continued.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: The engagement activity in this subject teaches exactly the investigate-and-act cycle CAS wants, which makes these students unusually good at designing a service project. The rule still holds: the engagement activity belongs to the subject and the CAS project has to be separate work.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: The two core components that carry marks, sharing a calendar with CAS. Worth listing here because the final CAS interview and the Extended Essay deadline usually land in the same term, and the component with no marks is the one that gets abandoned.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.regionsIntro: What stalls a CAS programme differs by area, because what is practically available differs. These notes describe what families in each part of the city actually run into.

regions.name: Jumeirah 1, 2 and 3
regions.note: Dense school provision and well-established CAS programmes with structured platforms and monthly checkpoints. Students here rarely lack activity or creativity; what they lack is service with an identified need rather than an afternoon at an event, which is what the final interview probes.

regions.name: Al Sufouh, Knowledge Village and Media City
regions.note: Proximity to universities and media organisations makes genuinely interesting creativity and service projects possible — workshops, mentoring, media production for a community organisation. The practical constraint is securing a named contact at an organisation the school accepts.

regions.name: Al Mizhar, Al Warqa and Mirdif
regions.note: Long-established schools with large cohorts and advisers carrying many students each. Portfolios here tend to be rich in experiences and thin in reflections, so an evidence-mapping session usually finds several outcomes already met but never recorded.

regions.name: The Sustainable City and Remraam
regions.note: Communities with their own environmental and community infrastructure, which produces some of the strongest CAS projects we see — a continuing commitment inside the community rather than a one-off event. The risk is a project that is organised for the student rather than by them.

regions.name: Dubai Sports City and Victory Heights
regions.note: Academies and clubs on the doorstep, so the activity strand is covered by default and often over-represented. These students need creativity and service deliberately planned, and the mentoring question is usually how to turn existing sport into a service commitment such as coaching younger players.

regions.name: Dubai South and Expo City
regions.note: Newer residential areas with longer journeys to the central school clusters, where weekday service commitments are hard to sustain. Projects that run at weekends or online, and that are properly documented, hold up better than ambitious weekday plans that lapse by November.

regions.name: Satwa and Al Karama
regions.note: Older, denser neighbourhoods near the centre with a mix of curricula. Many students here have genuine community involvement through family and neighbourhood networks that they do not think counts, and frequently it does once the need, the learning and the reflection are articulated.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches 2 and Mudon
regions.note: Villa communities with heavy HL loads and long school days. CAS here is usually the component with the least time, so the useful work is finding outcomes inside commitments the student already has rather than adding new ones in DP2.

schoolClusters.city: Al Sufouh, Knowledge Village and Dubai Media City
schoolClusters.note: Established Diploma cohorts close to the university and media cluster, which widens what a credible service or creativity commitment can look like. CAS systems here are generally structured, with the interview dates published in advance.

schoolClusters.city: Jumeirah and Satwa
schoolClusters.note: Long-running schools with strong co-curricular provision, so creativity and activity are usually well covered. The service strand and the one-month project are where students in this cluster most often need planning help.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Al Mizhar
schoolClusters.note: Large cohorts with advisers supporting many students at once. Portfolios from this cluster tend to be full of activity and short on recorded reflection, which an evidence-mapping session usually resolves quickly.

dubai/ib-dp-cas-tutor.modesIntro: CAS mentoring is short by design. These are the four shapes families in Dubai actually need, and the first one resolves most cases in a single session.

modes.title: Evidence mapping session
modes.description: One session that lists everything the student already does and maps it against the seven learning outcomes. Most students have met four or five outcomes without recording them, so the output is usually a short list of genuine gaps plus a set of reflections the student now knows to write. This is the session that resolves most CAS anxiety.
bullets: Every current commitment listed, including things done outside school
Each of the seven outcomes marked as evidenced, partly evidenced or missing
Double-counting with assessed coursework identified and separated
A written gap list the student can act on without further sessions

modes.title: CAS project design
modes.description: One or two sessions to design a project that satisfies the one-month duration and the collaboration requirement, and that the student can actually sustain. Work covers the investigation and preparation stages properly, because projects fail at planning rather than at execution.
bullets: A real identified need rather than an assumed one
Collaboration specified: who else, doing what, and when
Duration planned beyond the one-month minimum for safety
Demonstration planned at the start, not improvised at the end

modes.title: Reflection coaching
modes.description: A session on what a reflection has to contain to be worth the time: what happened, how the student responded, what they would do differently, and what they now understand about the outcome in question. Students write; the mentor questions and reads. Quality beats volume, and a portfolio of thirty thin entries is weaker than ten real ones.
bullets: The difference between a diary entry and a reflection, with examples
Reflections tied to named outcomes rather than written generically
Written at the time, not reconstructed months later
Every word the student's own, always

modes.title: Interview preparation
modes.description: Short preparation before one of the three documented interviews, particularly the final one. The mentor runs the questions a coordinator is likely to ask, checks the portfolio against the outcomes, and identifies anything that will be queried while there is still time to address it.
bullets: Portfolio checked outcome by outcome before the meeting
Likely coordinator questions rehearsed honestly
Gaps named plainly, including those that cannot now be filled
A short plan for the weeks between interview and completion

sections.heading: What CAS actually requires, and what it does not
paragraphs: CAS asks for four things. The student must engage in a range of experiences across creativity, activity and service over a period of at least eighteen months. They must provide evidence of having achieved all seven learning outcomes. They must complete a CAS project lasting at least one month that involves collaboration. And they must attend three documented interviews with the school's CAS coordinator or adviser, at the beginning, around the end of the first year, and at the end of the programme.

It does not ask for a number of hours. The hour requirement that older guidance quoted was removed, and nothing numerical replaced it. What replaced it is a reasonable balance across the three strands, judged by the coordinator, evidenced in the portfolio. This change is still working its way through conversations in Dubai staff rooms and family WhatsApp groups, and students continue to log hours as though the total were the deliverable. The total is not the deliverable; the evidence is.

It also does not ask for anything to be assessed. There is no mark, no grade and no moderation. The portfolio is not submitted to the IB for marking; it is the evidence the coordinator uses to determine that the requirement has been met. That is why CAS cannot be improved in the final month in the way an essay can. Evidence has to have accumulated while the experiences were happening, and a portfolio assembled retrospectively reads exactly like one assembled retrospectively.

What it does require, firmly, is completion. A student who does not complete CAS does not receive the Diploma, regardless of subject grades, TOK, or the Extended Essay. Every Dubai family should know that sentence by the end of the first term of DP1, because by DP2 the cost of learning it is measured in weeks that are already allocated elsewhere.
bullets: A minimum of eighteen months across creativity, activity and service
Evidence of all seven learning outcomes, not simply participation

sections.heading: The seven learning outcomes and what counts as evidence
paragraphs: The seven outcomes are the whole specification, and most students have never read them in one place. They cover identifying strengths and areas for growth, taking on new challenges and developing new skills, initiating and planning an experience, showing commitment and perseverance, demonstrating the skills and benefits of working collaboratively, engaging with issues of global significance, and recognising and considering the ethics of choices and actions. A student must show evidence of all seven across their programme, not one each term.

Evidence is the word that does the work. Participation is not evidence of initiative, and attendance is not evidence of perseverance. What satisfies an outcome is a record showing the student doing the thing the outcome names: a plan they wrote before an event, a message chain showing them organising other people, a reflection written mid-commitment describing why they wanted to stop and did not. Photographs are weak evidence on their own, which surprises students, because a photograph shows presence rather than contribution.

In practice most students in Dubai have already met four or five outcomes through things they do anyway — club sport, music, a family volunteering commitment, a school council role — and recorded none of them against an outcome. One mapping session usually converts that into a short, specific gap list. The outcomes that genuinely need designing are almost always initiating and planning, engagement with global significance, and the ethics of choices and actions, because those three require deliberate thought rather than continued participation.

The outcome on ethics is the one coordinators probe hardest at the final interview and the one students answer worst. It does not require a moral essay. It requires the student to describe a decision they actually faced in a CAS experience — who benefited, who was excluded, whether the help offered was what was needed — and what they concluded. A real small example beats a general statement about the importance of ethics every time.

sections.heading: The CAS project: one month, collaboration, and where it stalls
paragraphs: The CAS project is the one structural requirement beyond the outcomes: a challenge of at least one month's duration that involves collaboration and addresses one or more strands. Students read that as a month-long activity and plan accordingly, which is why so many projects fail. A month is the minimum envelope, and inside it the project is supposed to pass through investigation, preparation, action, reflection and demonstration. Compressed into four weeks with no preparation, it becomes an event with a reflection attached.

Collaboration is the second trap. Working alongside other people is not collaboration; collaboration means a shared goal with interdependent roles, which produces the disagreement and negotiation the outcome is actually about. The projects that document collaboration well are the ones where someone had to be persuaded, a plan had to change, or a role had to be reassigned. A project where the student did everything and others attended is a solo project with witnesses.

The third failure is scope. Ambitious projects — a charity, a city-wide campaign, a fundraising target — generate impressive plans and stall on permissions, insurance, licensing and adult availability. In the UAE, community organisations and charities operate under licence and schools maintain their own lists of organisations they will accept, so a project requiring a new external partnership needs the school's approval before any time is invested. Ask the coordinator first; it takes one email and prevents a month of wasted effort.

What works in Dubai is usually smaller and continuing: a weekly coaching session for younger players at a club the student already belongs to, a sustained initiative inside a residential community, a skills workshop run repeatedly for the same group rather than once for an audience. These satisfy duration naturally, generate real collaboration, and produce reflections that have something in them.
